stories.headline: Bolarum arms theft accused claims eight others helped him steal the cache
stories.deck: Mallesh allegedly planned to sell the stolen arms and ammunition after the theft. Now police have opened a fresh line of investigation into prospective buyers
stories.bodyText:
The 10-day police custody of former Army Havaldar Upputholla Mallesh, accused of stealing 12 firearms and over 1,800 rounds of ammunition from the 20 Battalion, Madras Regiment premises at Bolarum, will end on October 1, with his questioning throwing up claims about the involvement of more persons in the theft.
During interrogation, Mallesh allegedly claimed that eight others had helped him steal the cache from the Army premises. The persons he named include some security guards, and investigators are verifying their alleged roles in the theft.
The disclosure marks a shift from Mallesh’s earlier claim that he had acted alone.
Investigators have also learnt that while a grudge against his former superiors was allegedly the primary motive behind the theft, Mallesh also intended to make money by selling the stolen firearms and ammunition.
He was allegedly looking for prospective buyers for the weapons after stealing them, a line that investigators are now examining as part of the questioning.
Mallesh was taken into police custody on September 22 after a Secunderabad court granted investigators 10 days to question him over the theft, his motive and the possible involvement of others.

stories.headline: Asian Games 2026 India’s medallists: Full list of winners
stories.deck: Here’s the full list of Indian medallists at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games 2026 categorised by sport
stories.bodyText:
The 2026 Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games are underway in Japan. India is currently placed at the 8th spot on the medals’ table with 60 medals. China is leading the table with 277 medals. Japan is second with 200 medals and Republic of Korea is third with 103 medals.
India’s Dharmveer Chaudhary, Manu T.S., Jay Kumar and Vishal T.K. clinched the bronze medal in the men’s 4x400m relay at the Asian Games.
India’s Sunil Kumar clinched bronze in the Greco-Roman 87kg category at the Asian Games 2026, becoming the first Indian Greco-Roman wrestler to win two medals at the Games.
Kynan Darius Chenai and Neeru Dhanda staged a superb comeback to beat Qatar and claim gold in the trap mixed team event. The Indian pair finished with an Asian-record score of 34, securing India’s third gold medal of the day.
India edged China 238-237 to clinch gold in the men’s compound archery event, completing a clean sweep of all three compound events. Earlier, the women’s team of Jyothi Surekha Vennam, Prithika Pradeep and Chikitha Taniparthi defeated China to win gold, while India beat South Korea in a shoot-off in the mixed team final to seal another gold and secure a place at the LA 2028 Olympics.
Indian boxer Priya Ghanghas signed off with a bronze medal after going down to former world champion China’s Yang Chengyu in the 60kg semifinal and similarly, Kapil Pokhariya bowed out with a bronze medal after losing 1-4 to Uzbekistan’s Turabek Khabibullaev in the men’s 90kg semifinal.
On Tuesday (September 29, 2026), the quartet of Kiran Pahal, M.R. Poovamma, Prachi Choudhary and Vithya Ramraj won India’s first and only track-and-field gold medal at the Asian Games in Nagoya.
Indian boxer Narender Berwal won the men’s +90kg bronze medal at the 2026 Asian Games after losing to reigning world champion Aibek Oralbay of Kazakhstan in the semi-finals on Tuesday (September 30, 2026).
Gulveer Singh added a third medal to his tally at the 2026 Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, clinching bronze in the men’s 5000m on Tuesday.
India’s mixed 4x100m relay quartet of Gurindervir Singh, Sneha S.S., Animesh Kujur and Harita Bhadra clinched bronze at the Asian Games.
India’s Pooja Singh secured the bronze medal in the women’s high jump at the 2026 Asian Games on Tuesday after clearing 1.84m in the final.
The quartet of Manu T.S., Dharmveer Choudhary, Jay Kumar and Vishal T.K. clinched bronze in the men’s 4x400m relay final on Tuesday.
Neeru Dhanda scripted history on Tuesday (September 29, 2026), becoming the first Indian shooter to win an Asian Games gold medal in the women’s individual trap event, while also breaking the continental record in the process.
Indian shooters Neeru Dhanda, Aashima Ahlawat and Manisha Keer clinched silver in the women’s trap team event at the Asian Games.
On September 28, 2026, Vithya Ramraj won a bronze medal in 400 M hurdles in a sensational run that clocked 54.75 seconds and broke her own national record she had jointly held with athlete PT Usha.
Murali Sreeshankar and Gulveer Singh claimed silver medals in the long jump and 1500m, respectively, while Parul Chaudhary secured bronze in the women’s 5000m, adding a second medal to her Aichi-Nagoya campaign.
India also bagged two medals in the javelin throw, with Yash Vir Singh winning silver and Rohit Yadav taking bronze, behind Sri Lanka’s Rumesh Tharanga.
Earlier that day, Indian shooter Esha Singh clinched a silver medal in the women’s 25m pistol individual competition.
Pincky Balhara became the first Indian to win two Kurash medals at the Asian Games after clinching bronze on Monday (September 28, 2026), following a 0-5 semifinal defeat to South Korea’s Sumin Mo in the women’s 78kg event.
On Sunday (September 27, 2026), India’s Abhay Singh settled for an Asian Games silver medal after going down against Eain Yow Ng of Malaysia in the men’s singles final of the squash competition, and junior world champion Anahat Singh similarly secured a hard-fought Silver in the women’s singles final against Malaysia’s Sivasangari Subramaniam.
Harita Bhadra clinched bronze in the women’s 200m at the Asian Games. Long jumper Ancy Sojan secured silver in the women’s long jump, while Sarvesh Kushare claimed silver in the men’s high jump.
Tejaswin Shankar, meanwhile, secured his second Asian Games medal, winning bronze in the decathlon following the two-day competition.
Parul Chaudhary bettered her personal best on her way to bronze in the women’s 3000m steeplechase at the Asian Games.
On Saturday (September 26), India’s Sawan Barwal won a silver medal in the men’s marathon. India’s women’s kabaddi team extended their dominance at the Asian Games securing yet another gold medal after a thrilling 37-34 win over Iran in the finals. The men’s hockey team continued it’s winning streak, defeating Japan by 2-0, securing the semifinal berth in the big-ticket sports event.
Simultaneously, the squash squad led by teen-sensation Anahat Singh and Abhay Shetty in singles category stormed into the final game. The duo will be competing for a gold medal in their final game on Sunday.
Women’s 50m rifle 3P team comprising of Vidarsa Vinod, Ashi Chouksey, Tilottama Sen won the silver medal. Mixed squash doubles team including Joshana Chinappa, Velavan Senthilkumar clinched the bronze medal.
On Friday (September 25), the duo of Manush Shah and Diya Chitale secured a historic bronze medal in table tennis mixed doubles after stunning the world No. 4 pair from Hong Kong to enter the semi-finals.
Baranica Elangovan entered her name in the record books by winning a historic bronze medal for India in the women’s pole vault event at the Asian Games
Indian long-distance runner Gulveer Singh upgraded his Asian Games medal from bronze to silver in the men’s 10,000m.
India’s Manpreet Kaur clinched the bronze medal in women’s shot put competition of the Asian Games with an effort of 17.17m in Nagoya on Friday (September 25).
Kamaljeet and Suruchi Singh won gold in the mixed team 10m air pistol event. The Indian team, comprising Aishwary Pratap Singh Tomar, Rudranksh Patil and Niraj Kumar, won silver in the men’s 50m rifle 3P team event.
The Indian 4x400m mixed relay quartet of Vishal T.K., M.R. Poovamma, Manu T.S. and Vithya Ramraj earned a silver medal in the final at the Paloma Mizuho Stadium.
Manpreet Kaur clinched a bronze medal in the Women’s Shot Put final with a season-best throw of 17.17 meters.
The duo of Manush Shah and Diya Chitale secured a historic bronze in Table Tennis Mixed Doubles after stunning the world No. 4 pair from Hong Kong to enter the semi-finals.
Seema Kumari, competing in her first Asiad, won a bronze medal in the 10,000m at the Asian Games, 16 years after Preeja Sreedharan and Kavita Raut’s historic gold-silver double in 2010.
Manipur’s Naorem Roshibina Devi won her third consecutive Asian Games medal, clinching silver after losing to Zhang Xiaoyu in the women’s 60kg wushu final on Thursday (September 24, 2026).
Jay Meena secured India’s first-ever soft tennis medal at the Asian Games, fetching a bronze after losing to Japan’s Takuya Kurosaka in the men’s singles semifinals. Star Indian weightlifter Mirabai Chanu completed her medal collection, winning a silver medal in the women’s 49kg event in the Asian Games.
Lakshya Sen and Ayush Shetty faltered against higher-ranked opponents as the Indian men’s team concluded with a bronze medal after losing 1-3 to their rivals, China, in the semifinals.
The Indian Women’s Cricket Team clinched a historic victory at the Karogi Athletic Park in Nisshin, Aichi. Facing off against Sri Lanka in a high-stakes final, the Women in Blue triumphed to secure India’s very first gold medal of the tournament.
Meanwhile, shooters have led the charge for India. The women’s skeet team, comprising Raiza Dhillon, Maheshwari Chauhan and Parinaaz Dhaliwal, won a bronze with a combined score of 331 here on September 23, 2026.
Experienced rifle shooter Elavenil Valarivan played a starring role in the country’s double-silver haul in the women’s 10m air rifle competition. Elavenil, one of India’s most accomplished rifle shooters, helped the country secure silver in the team event along with Sonam Maskar and Vidarsa Vinod. She then went on to add an individual silver.
For the men’s side, teenager Himanshu Dhillon produced a superb performance to win silver, while former world champion Rudrankksh Patil clinched bronze as India secured two individual podium finishes in the men’s 10m air rifle event. The two then teamed up with Parth Mane to win another silver in the team event, finishing just behind China.
After an impressive start in shooting, India also managed to script history in Mixed Martial Arts (MMA), with Suchika Tariyal winning the nation’s first-ever bronze medal for MMA at the Asian Games.
A contingent of 501 Indian athletes, comprising 267 men and 234 women, is competing across 36 disciplines in the 2026 edition. Apart from shooting, athletics and archery too are expected to add to the medal tally. India is also defending both the men’s and women’s titles in cricket and kabaddi.

stories.headline: Amazon founder Jeff Bezos puts deposit on LA’s most expensive penthouse
stories.deck: Jeff Bezos has made waves in the real estate market with a $200 million deposit for a stunning penthouse in Aman Beverly Hills. This expansive 31,000 square foot residence boasts lavish features like a rooftop swimming pool and private cinema, all designed by acclaimed Kerry Hill Architects. If finalized, it could smash records for condo sales in Los Angeles by 2028, adding to Bezos's impressive…
stories.bodyText:
Amazon founder Jeff Bezos has reportedly placed a deposit on what could become the most expensive condo ever sold in Los Angeles, according to a report by Luxury Launches. The property consists of six-bedrooms and 17,000-square-foot penthouse at the upcoming Aman Beverly Hills. Priced at $200 million, or nearly $12,000 per square foot, the residence crowns one of two residential towers in the luxury development, scheduled to open in 2028. Designed by Kerry Hill Architects, the penthouse spans more than 31,000 square feet of combined interior and exterior space.
All about Jeff Bezos’ new expensive penthouse
The penthouse sits atop one of two residential towers at Aman Beverly Hills, an upcoming hotel development featuring Aman-branded residences and a private Aman Club, set on ten acres of botanical gardens and slated to open in 2028. Priced at $200 million, or nearly $12,000 per square foot, the unit would set a new record for L.A. condo sales if the purchase closes — regardless of whether Bezos or another billionaire ultimately signs on the dotted line.
According to The Hollywood Reporter, the residence spans more than 31,000 square feet when combining interior and exterior space, crowning a 28-story tower with views stretching across the Los Angeles Country Club, the Hollywood Hills, Downtown L.A., 
and the Pacific Ocean. Designed by Kerry Hill Architects, the interiors feature 22-foot ceilings and blend California mid-century modernism with Aman's signature Japanese-influenced restraint, built from stone, timber, and metal in muted tones.
The penthouse is layered between three separate levels of gardens and terraces, anchored by a 65-foot rooftop swimming pool with an attached Jacuzzi — a setup reminiscent of the amenities aboard a large superyacht, not unlike Bezos's own roughly $500 million vessel, Koru. Outdoor spaces include multiple fireplaces, dining terraces, lounges, and a yoga deck, alongside a private cinema. Residents also get privileged access to Aman's planned 100,000-square-foot standalone club, built around wellness, dining, fitness, and social programming — described as the first freestanding club of its kind for the brand.
A neighborhood of billionaires
If the deal closes, Bezos will add the Aman penthouse to his growing Los Angeles portfolio, which already includes the Jack Warner Estate purchased for $165 million. The Aman residence would serve as a holiday home, complementing his primary residence on Indian Creek Island.

stories.headline: 5.44 magnitude earthquake jolts Afghanistan’s Hindu Kush region
stories.bodyText:
A 5.44-magnitude earthquake jolted Afghanistan’s Hindu Kush region early Thursday, according to the GFZ German Research Centre for Geosciences.
The earthquake struck at 0129 GMT (6.59 am IST), with its epicentre initially located at 36.05 degrees north latitude and 68.87 degrees east longitude. The quake occurred at a depth of 10 km, making it a relatively shallow earthquake.
There were no immediate reports of casualties or damage.
The Hindu Kush is one of the most seismically active regions around Afghanistan and Pakistan. Earthquakes in the broader Hindu Kush-Pamir region can occur at both shallow and great depths, with some linked to complex tectonic activity beneath the mountain ranges.
The wider region lies within the zone of continuing collision between the Indian and Eurasian plates, which has produced frequent earthquakes across the Himalaya, Hindu Kush and surrounding mountain systems.
The shallow depth of Thursday’s earthquake is notable because earthquakes occurring closer to the surface can produce stronger shaking near the epicentre than much deeper earthquakes of similar magnitude.
The Hindu Kush region has experienced several earthquakes in recent years, including moderate and deeper events recorded by international and regional seismological agencies.

briefs.headline: Trained canines to bolster crime detection in Andhra Pradesh
briefs.deck: 36 canines and their handlers complete 10-month training in detection of explosives, narcotics, cadavers and Search & Rescue operations
briefs.bodyText:
In an impressive live demonstration, trained canines of the Intelligence Security Wing (ISW) of the Andhra Pradesh Police showcased their capabilities on Wednesday.
Be it tactical assault routines or sniffing out narcotics concealed wrapped in complex packaging, the skilled pack of Belgian Malinois and Dutch Shepherds demonstrated their prowess.
Accompanied by their handlers, the canines demonstrated flawless discipline, agility, and specialised tactical skills at the passing-out parade of the 23rd batch of canines and their handlers at the Canine Training Centre on the A.P. Special Police’s 6th Battalion premises near Mangalagiri on Wednesday.
In total, 36 canines completed their 10-month training in detection of explosives, narcotics, cadavers and in assault and Search & Rescue (S&R).
Participating in the event, Home Minister V. Anitha praised the police canines for their role in the detection of crimes, boosting crime detection with the help of modern technologies and advanced forensic evidence processing.
Currently, 218 canines are serving the Police Department in the State, and 78 of them were trained in the last two years, she said.
“The canine wing of the police has proved their mettle in solving cases. They have played a key role in crubing the drug cases,” she said.
Director General of Police (DGP) Harish Kumar Gupta said canines have become the most reliable companions in policing. Canines trained in cadaver detection are being inducted into the A.P. State Disaster Response Force for the first time. The dog handlers and other staff are trained in advanced methods in coordination with the CRPF Dog Breeding & Training Centre in Taralu (Bengaluru). Belgian Malinois and Dutch Shepherds have been introduced for dual duties in accordance with internal security requirements,” he said.
DGP (CID) Ravishankar Ayyanar, Director General (ACB) Atul Singh, Additional DGs Mahesh Chandra Laddha (Intelligence) and N. Madhusudana Reddy (Law and Order), Inspectors General of Police B. Rajakumari, Kanthi Rana Tata and K.V. Mohan Rao and SP K. Arif Hafeez were present.

briefs.headline: Pilot attacked in flydubai altercation Indian
briefs.deck: At this early stage, the underlying reasons and motives behind this event are unknown and remain subject to a formal investigation, reads a press statement by flydubai
briefs.bodyText:
The captain who was attacked during an altercation inside the cockpit of a flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv on Wednesday (September 30, 2026) is an Indian national, Captain Smit Machchhar.
Mr. Machchaar was previously employed with SpiceJet
In a press statement, flydubai has called the incident aboard FZ 1073 “an altercation”.
“At this early stage, the underlying reasons and motives behind this event are unknown and remain subject to a formal investigation,” according to the press statement.
The airline said that the aircraft was successfully secured by on-duty flydubai crew travelling on the flight, who diverted and landed the aircraft safely at Tabuk Airport (TUU) in Saudi Arabia, and that all passengers and crew were safe and accounted for.
flydubai, in a statement, said that flights to and from Israel will be suspended while the investigation regarding the incident continues.
Praise from PM Modi, Netanyahu
Prime Ministers Narendra Modi and Benjamin Netanyahu said that Mr. Machchhar was a ‘hero’ for his intervention.
“In the face of the gravest danger and despite being seriously injured, he showed immense courage and an unwavering resolve to protect the lives of others. His valour helped save hundreds of lives and avert a great tragedy. India is proud of Captain Machchhar,” Mr. Modi said.
“My salute to the Indian pilot Captain Smit Machchhar for his extraordinary bravery. Despite being stabbed and seriously injured, he fought back, resisted, opened the cockpit door, and enabled passengers and crew to overpower the attacker — preventing a catastrophic mid-air disaster. He saved the lives of 174 people, including Israeli citizens and other nationals,” Mr. Netanyahu said in a statement.
Pilot Machchaar receiving necessary medical attention: Indian Embassy
The Indian Embassy in Riyadh said that it has been following the health condition of Mr. Machchhar along with the Consulate in Jeddah. “He is admitted in a hospital in Tabuk city in northwest Saudi Arabia and receiving necessary medical attention. A full update on his health is awaited but he is reported to be in stable condition,” the embassy posted on X.
“We hope that he recovers from his injuries at the earliest. We are in touch with his family and assure them that we will continue to follow up on his health with Saudi authorities and extend all possible assistance for his wellbeing.”

briefs.headline: U.S. Supreme Court clears way for Tennessee woman's imminent execution
briefs.deck: A decision by the U.S. Supreme Court late on September 30 cleared the way for Christa Pike to be given a lethal injection after hours of dramatic legal wrangling up and down the judicial system
briefs.bodyText:
A Tennessee woman was expected to be put to death Wednesday (September 30, 2026) for the murder of a high-school friend in what would be the first execution of a woman in that state in two centuries.
A decision by the U.S. Supreme Court late Wednesday (September 30, 2026) cleared the way for Christa Pike -- the only woman on the state's death row -- to be given a lethal injection after hours of dramatic legal wrangling up and down the judicial system.
A lawyer for Pike, Luke Ihnen, told AFP that there are no plans to file for further reprieve and that the execution "should start any minute if it hasn't already."
"We do not plan to file anything else," Mr. Ihnen said.
When Pike is given a lethal injection, she will become the first woman executed in the U.S. since 2023.
Pike had been scheduled for execution at 10:00 a.m. (1500 GMT) at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution, but it was halted barely an hour before by a lower court.
That court was set to review whether allegations that Pike was sexually abused as a child were fully considered in her original prosecution.
"The interests of justice and the finality of Pike's impending execution compel the entry of a short stay of execution in order to properly analyze the parties' fully briefed arguments," the lower court order said.
But the Supreme Court later said it could go ahead.
"The September 30, 2026 order of the United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit...granting a stay of execution is vacated," the Supreme Court order said.
Liberal Supreme Court Justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson all dissented.
"The Court's decision... unnecessarily prevents that [lower] court from giving due consideration to Pike's claim," the dissenting justices wrote.
"Worse, the court grants such extraordinary relief solely to allow the state to execute Pike before litigation over her conviction has properly run its course in the lower courts."
Mental health considerations
The case has sparked debate over capital punishment for young criminals.
Pike was 18 when she and her boyfriend beat and killed Colleen Slemmer, 19, at a job training camp for young people.
The killing gained national attention after Slemmer's body was found with a pentagram, often seen as a satanic symbol, carved in her chest.
Pike's lawyers argued she should be granted clemency due to her young age and mental health issues at the time of the killing.
"She was 18 when she committed her crime, and she was deeply mentally ill," they wrote in a clemency petition to Tennessee Governor Bill Lee, who said he would not intervene.
The U.S. Supreme Court had rejected Tuesday (September 29, 2026) an application for a stay of execution, which argued that Pike's history as a victim of sexual assault, post-traumatic stress disorder and a blood condition meant a lethal injection would cause "needless suffering."
Independent UN rights experts have urged the U.S. government and Tennessee authorities to "immediately halt" the execution and commute her death sentence.
"Pike's execution would mark the culmination of a trajectory of severe physical and psychological suffering marked by childhood abuse and nearly three decades of solitary confinement on death row," they said.
In the United States, only 18 women have been executed since 1976, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.

briefs.headline: India’s river interlinks may carry invasive species to more areas
briefs.deck: The Lower Ganga basin hosts 13-15 invasive alien species and could become a major source of invasives for the Mahanadi, home to 69 threatened species; water connections under the river interlinking project could also help aquatic pathogens to spread and flatten the unique biota that individual river basins boast today
briefs.bodyText:
The National River-Linking Project is the world’s most ambitious project of its kind to date, proposing to link 37 major river basins across India using 30 links, potentially redistributing around 174 billion cubic metres of water from ‘surplus’ to ‘deficit’ basins while generating some 34,000 MW of power.
Yet the Project has also raised serious concerns about its environmental costs. Experts have said the idea of ‘surplus’ and ‘deficit’ basins can mask seasonal and year-on-year variations in river flows, and that transferring water between basins can alter downstream flows, sediment transport, floodplains, deltas, and the habitats that depend on them. Dams, reservoirs, and canals can also break ecosystems up into pieces and disturb fish migration and other ecological processes.
Climate change has also been complicating assumptions about how much water a basin will reliably have available to transfer in the decades ahead. But it seems river-linking also poses another, less obvious problem.
‘Ecological highways’
Recently, researchers from the Ashoka Trust for Research in Ecology and the Environment (ATREE), Bengaluru, assessed the Project also possibly creating “ecological highways” that invasive species can travel on to new, ecologically sensitive areas.
Their findings were recently published in Scientific Reports.
Because of the ways in which India’s river basins are isolated from each other, many species in each one are endemic, meaning they inhabit a small area and are not found elsewhere on the planet. River links may then threaten them more than native species.
“There is no public or verifiable scientific basis that backs any of the claims of benefits of the National River-Linking Project, but more of a notional basis that if you connect a drier part to a wetter part of the country, there will be water balance, as opposed to how ecology actually works,” Siddharth Agarwal, director-founder of the Veditum India Foundation, a nonprofit working on environmental governance, said.
In the paper, the team showed that all Northeast and peninsular Indian basins are more vulnerable to biological invasions than those in Central and North India.
The Southwestern Ghats, Kaveri, Krishna Lower Ganga, and Brahmaputra basins support diverse habitats and complex ecological niches that host native species, threatened species, and invasive alien species.
‘Invasion hotspots’
“Right now, [the invasive alien species] are isolated, restricted to individual river basins,” the study’s lead author and ATREE senior fellow Aravind Neelavar Ananthram said. “By connecting rivers, we would not only introduce new species which are not naturally found but also increase the vulnerability of the native species that cannot compete with the invasive alien species.”
This finding is consistent with research worldwide, which has suggested that biodiversity hotspots can accumulate more invasive alien species, thus compromising the long-term prospects of native species and themselves turning into ‘invasion hotspots’.
For example, the Lower Ganga basin hosts 13-15 invasive alien species, and could become a major source of invasives for the Mahanadi, which is home to 69 threatened species. In fact, this is one of the Project’s most ecologically sensitive links, and it could increase the risk of extinction for the threatened species.
Water connections under the Project could also help aquatic pathogens to spread, disrupt the migratory routes of fish, and flatten the unique biota that individual river basins boast today.
“Fishes in one river basin may be well adapted or immune to the pathogens it harbours, while species in other basins may not be able to protect themselves against such pathogens,” Dr. Ananthram said. “If one reduces the water flow by taking out water from one river and putting it into another, the downstream water flow will be reduced. As a consequence, the downstream biodiversity will be severely affected and there is a high chance that the endemic species in the lower reaches might go extinct.”
“The river linking project is being sold as a solution (at least for the Ken-Betwa) to water scarcity (in Bundelkhand), but can it really serve the objectives that it is proposing?” Mr. Agarwal asked. “There is no way for us to verify. It is more of a capital investment than an ecological one.”
In need of foresight
“Rivers like the Ken have sand of great ecological value. But when the Ken-Betwa link is live, large quantities of water will be moved away from the river, lowering the flow volume and reducing sediment production rates in the river,” Mr. Agarwal said. “That could ultimately reduce the biodiversity in the river and potentially even trigger a food chain collapse.”
The Project’s consequences may also extend to downstream nations.
“Right now, we have only considered 15 freshwater invasive species for which data is available,” Dr. Ananthram said. “If one looks at all species across India, including terrestrial and marine systems, it would be approximately 350 to 400 species in different stages of invasion. Developed economies like Australia and in Europe have very strong policies for invasive alien species. It is an urgent need that India comes up with a specific policy targeted to regulate, manage and control” such species.
Embedding evidence-based management of river basins into national infrastructure planning could provide ecological foresight.
“The health risks, biodiversity, wildlife, and economic costs of [the Project] to India, especially for the agro-economy, farmers’ livelihoods, and fisheries, are matters of urgent attention,” he added. “While the government’s intention might be good to address water deficit, development plans and policy decisions should be holistic, addressing the ecological impact, the effect on biodiversity, and people’s lives.”
Jhinook Mitra is an independent researcher and ecologist, currently with the Nature Conservation Foundation, Bengaluru.

briefs.headline: 'Hero in a way': Trump hails stabbed Flydubai Indian pilot, calls co-pilot 'whack job'
briefs.bodyText:
US President 
Donald Trump
 has hailed Indian Flydubai captain Smit Machchhar as “a hero” after he was stabbed by his co-pilot during a mid-air attack on an Israel-bound flight.
“In a way he was a hero,” Trump said of Machchhar, saying the badly wounded pilot still managed to open the cockpit door and call for help.
Trump, while speaking about the incident, also described the co-pilot as “perhaps a terrorist or perhaps a whack job”, as the motive behind the attack remained under investigation.
The Dubai-to-Tel Aviv Flydubai flight plunged thousands of feet during the confrontation in the cockpit, triggering panic among passengers. The aircraft was eventually diverted and landed safely in Saudi Arabia.
US says no credible threats after Flydubai incident
US homeland security secretary Markwayne Mullin said there were currently “no credible threats” directed at the United States following the incident.
“We have no credible threats to us right now. We take every incident like this very serious, and we continue to look at the procedures that we have in place and continue to make sure the American people are safe,” Mullin said, according to Fox News.
The statement came as aviation authorities reviewed security procedures following the attack on the Flydubai flight.
Indian captain helped passengers overpower attacker
The captain was identified as Indian national Smit Machchhar, a seasoned pilot with more than 13 years of commercial aviation experience. He has around 9,750 flying hours, predominantly on Boeing 737 aircraft, and previously spent about 11 years with SpiceJet, where he served as a Line Training Captain, news agency ANI reported.
Despite suffering serious stab wounds, Machchhar reportedly managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers and crew to enter and restrain the attacker.

stories.headline: Building community in Bengaluru, one ghost at a time
stories.deck: An interview with Tarun Sridharan, the founder of the Ghost Story Collective, a community-driven storytelling organisation focused on raw, unscripted paranormal events
stories.bodyText:
It began at a dinner party in Hyderabad. By the end of the evening, attended by people from around the world, Tarun Sridharan, who was at the party, says. “We started telling ghost stories, personal ones,”
Tarun, an Indian-American litigator and marketing professional, is also the creator of Odd Compass, an animated YouTube channel focusing heavily on South and Southeast Asian history. “We had such a great time. It almost felt like telling tales around a campfire.”
It got him thinking about the absence of storytelling events. “Earlier, you would go down to your local tavern, where a storyteller would hold you captive with his tales. And maybe some other people would join in to start telling their stories, and that would be the entertainment for the evening,” says the Bengaluru-based Tarun.
This was the genesis of the Ghost Story Collective, a community-driven storytelling organisation focused on raw, unscripted paranormal phenomena. “I thought it would be great to invite people to either be listeners or to tell a ghost story,” he says. In his view, it would also be a great way to foster bonding, because once you put yourself out there, “it is natural to be able to talk with other people, and maybe make new friends.”
Restricting the stories to paranormal tales offers an anchor of sorts, believes Tarun. “Ghost stories describe the diversity of the human experience so deeply,” he says, adding that the participants draw on many cultural and historical elements. Additionally, “We all like to sit around and tell ghost stories. It is just a lot of fun.”
Since July this year, the collective has had around 10 events across three cities, Bengaluru, Delhi and Hyderabad, says Tarun, describing the format of these events: “When you sign up, you can buy a ticket (priced at ₹ 299) either as a storyteller or a listener: they cost the same, but it lets us know what you are planning.” Depending on the show’s length, there can be a maximum of eight tickets for storytellers, but there are also a few wild card slots. “If you are inspired by the stories there, you can raise your hand, and, depending on time, we will allow you to speak.”
The sessions begin with a quick introduction, “where we just talk about what we think about ghost stories: the historical, cultural and psychosocial aspects of them,” says Tarun. Then they invite people to start telling their stories, interspersing the storytelling sessions with discussions about the paranormal.
For example, vampires are often associated with Western mythology, but in Indian ghost mythology, too, many creatures are blood-sucking or flesh-eating, he points out. “The mythos is so steeped in blood being a source of power and life, almost exactly the same as the Eastern European myths. Vampiric mythology is so popular worldwide, but Indian vampiric myths aren’t given the same attention.”
The storytelling and discussions are followed by a short socialising session, says Tarun, whose larger goal is to build a community and meet more people through this initiative. “I feel like Bengaluru is a bit more introverted, as a city, and that is why events like this here do so well,” he says.
Many people attending these events are migrants and transplants who often struggle with social isolation. “It provides space for them to meet new people. Storytelling, in my view, is a source of human connection,” says Tarun, recalling how people often spent time outside the venue, hanging out. . “So many people seemed to be making new friends; I was shocked by how effective it was.”
He now hopes to take this format to other cities, “especially Calcutta, because I feel that everyone from there seems to be into ghost stories. A friend of mine is willing to host in a cafe there, so that is already underway,” says Tarun, who feels that the key to expanding it is to find a few hosts in other cities, too, to do this on a semi-regular basis. “The idea is maybe two events per month to start with.”
He also, at some point, wants to do events that bring together history and heritage, the focus of Odd Compass, and ghost stories. “People have this sense that a ghost story is a fun thing that someone tells, and it can be that, but I also want them to experience how culturally significant these things can be, in some way. I’d love to be able to do more heritage-based events associated with them,” says Tarun.
To know more about the Ghost Story Collective, check out their Instagram page

Greater Bengaluru Development Minister Krishna Byre Gowda on Wednesday (September 30) revealed that the government may explore a Metro connection between Dommasandra and Hope Farm in the future while inspecting State Highway-35 and surrounding stretches on the eastern fringes of the city.

Mr. Gowda directed the Karnataka Road Development Corporation Limited (KRDCL) to fix SH-35 and surrounding stretches within two to three months, while stressing the need to plan road works keeping future Metro expansion and other transport projects in mind.
He acknowledged that several connecting roads to SH-35 are narrower and could pose a greater congestion threat in the coming years. Mr. Gowda particularly ordered the fixing of the Sarjapur Road–Dommasandra–Gunjur–Varthur–Balagere corridor within two to three months.
During an inspection of the corridor and surrounding areas, Mr. Gowda reviewed road works, drainage, traffic management, land acquisition, electricity infrastructure, and other civic works.

Near the Varthur Lake bund, where two roads converge, Mr. Gowda noticed that no work had been carried out despite land being available. He lashed out at the engineer and directed that work be started immediately. Further, he pointed out that several establishments between Gunjur and Dommasandra had allegedly encroached upon more than eight feet of roadside space and sought action against such encroachments. He also reprimanded officials for allowing the encroachments to take place.
He further directed officials to identify and address waterlogging points and traffic bottlenecks immediately. stories.headline: Bengaluru sees flooded roads, fallen trees & traffic snarls
stories.bodyText:
Bengaluru: A spell of heavy evening rain brought parts of Bengaluru to a standstill Wednesday, flooding roads, choking traffic and leaving motorists battling waterlogged stretches across several parts of the city.
The downpour, accompanied by strong winds, brought down trees at multiple locations, further disrupting evening peak-hour traffic. India Meteorological Department (IMD) officials said the city received 1.6mm of rainfall until 8.30pm. “However, rain was intense in eastern parts of the city -- over 18mm,” an official said. According to KSNDMC, however, Bengaluru received an average of 10mm rainfall.
The city was overcast since morning, but rain intensified towards evening, quickly turning several arterial roads, underpasses and low-lying stretches into waterlogged corridors. Peenya flyover, Hebbal Ring Road and several underpasses were among the worst affected. Water accumulated near Hebbal Ring Road, triggering long queues of vehicles.
Commuters reported waterlogging near Hoodi Metro station. Varun Rao, a commuter, posted on X that there were hardly any drains between the Metro station and Hoodi circle, resulting in rainwater flowing directly onto the main road. He said pedestrians were forced to wade through ankle- to knee-deep water.
Vidyashilp railway underpass in Yelahanka, Rashtrothana flyover, Choudappa Layout and Thanisandra Road were inundated, throwing traffic out of gear. A large tree was uprooted near Vijnana Nagar, bringing traffic towards Kaggadasapura to a halt. Another tree reportedly fell near Vidhya Soudha School, adding to the evening chaos. Water stagnated along the stretch from Rainbow Hospital towards Karthik Nagar, between Yelahanka BSF and Airport Road, and from Mahadevapura towards Lorry Junction, making commuting difficult.
Similar scenes were reported on Vibgyor Road in Whitefield, where waterlogging left vehicles stranded and some motorists struggling to negotiate the flooded stretch. Sahakara Nagar too witnessed significant water accumulation, with clogged drains leaving roads inundated. Traffic moved slowly through several neighbourhoods, while minor jams were reported at multiple locations.

stories.headline: Mangaluru-Goa Vande Bharat to be extended till B’luru soon
stories.bodyText:
Bengaluru: Railway ministry will soon extend Mangaluru-Madgaon Vande Bharat Express to Bengaluru, meeting two long-standing demands from rail users for premium train services connecting Karnataka’s capital with Mangaluru and Goa.
TOI has learnt that railway minister 
Ashwini Vaishnaw
 wrote to two MPs from Karnataka, Brijesh Chowta and Vishweshwar Hegde Kageri, earlier this month, communicating the decision to extend the train route.
Currently, 20646/20645 Mangaluru Central–Madgaon Vande Bharat Express runs six days a week, with no service Thursdays. According to its timetable, the train takes a little less than six hours to complete a single-direction journey.
Proposals to operate Vande Bharat between Bengaluru and Goa were first initiated by South Western Railway (SWR), Konkan Railway Corporation Limited (KRCL) and Southern Railway (SR), in Feb. They suggested the train originate from Yeshwantpur in Bengaluru at 6:05am and reach Madgaon in Goa by 7:15pm, taking 13 hours. Currently, trains between Bengaluru and Goa take around 15 hours.
Vaishnaw said the extension will make the train terminate at Yeshwantpur Junction, traversing through Kabaka Puttur and Subrahmanya Road stations. 
It will become the first self-propelled train to travel along the 55-km ghats section between Sakleshpur and Subrahmanya Road after it was electrified in late 2025.
Though the proposal initially suggested a bypass without entering Mangaluru Central station, the plan has now been changed. For Bengaluru-Mangaluru route, two trial runs using a 16-car rake were conducted in Sept, and the train took less than seven hours to complete the journey.
The number of commercial stops in the final timetable will determine the total running time. While timings are yet to be finalised, the train will run with entirely new numbers, 26655/26656 in both directions. It will also be renamed Yeshwantpur-Madgaon Vande Bharat Express. The commencement date of the extended service has not been finalised; SWR officials did not comment on the matter.

briefs.headline: Karnataka SIR: Civil society report flags large-scale voter deletions, ground-level discrepancies
briefs.deck: Report cites 1.08 crore reduction in draft roll; 100-booth survey alleges voters marked shifted, absent or dead
briefs.bodyText:
An investigation report by the Anti-SIR Alliance and the Citizens’ Vote Protection Committee has flagged what it describes as large-scale deletions and discrepancies in Karnataka’s electoral rolls following the Special Intensive Revision (SIR).
The report, based on electoral-roll data, a survey of Booth Level Officers (BLOs) and ground verification across 100 polling booths in 25 districts, says Karnataka’s electorate fell from 5,52,49,719 voters in 2025 to 4,44,53,380 in the draft roll — a reduction of about 19.5%.
The organisations have raised questions over the scale of the deletions, particularly the large number of voters categorised as “Shifted” and “Absent”.
‘Shifted’ category
According to the report, 65,45,679 voters were classified as “Shifted”, 16,39,864 as “Dead”, 15,17,042 as “Absent”, 7,09,870 as “Duplicate” and 3,83,884 under “Others”.
The report says the “Shifted” category warrants particular scrutiny, arguing that people who move for employment or change rented accommodation should have an opportunity to transfer their registration rather than being removed from the rolls.
The committee also points to the difficulties faced by migrant workers who may not be present at home when BLOs conduct verification.
100-booth survey
The Citizens’ Vote Protection Committee said its house-to-house verification found instances where voters living at their registered addresses had allegedly been marked as “Shifted” or “Absent”. It also claimed that some living voters had been recorded under the “Dead” category.
The report found that some eligible voters did not receive enumeration forms and that several voters were unaware that their names had been removed from the draft roll.
The organisations have acknowledged that their survey covered only a small proportion of Karnataka’s polling booths and called for wider verification.
Bengaluru figures questioned
The report has separately highlighted Bengaluru, where it says the electorate fell from 1,11,16,111 to 48,48,574 in the draft roll.
The committee has questioned the scale of the reduction in a city that has witnessed substantial population growth and inward migration and has sought a detailed official explanation.
Marginalised communities
The report claimed that deletions were particularly high in some backward districts and constituencies with sizable SC, ST and Muslim populations.
It pointed out that women were disproportionately represented in the “Shifted” category, partly because of changes in residence after marriage.
The organisations have raised concerns about the impact of the revision on nomadic communities, Adivasis, Dalits, migrant workers, Muslims and people living in informal settlements.
BLOs report workload pressures
The report also highlighted the burden on BLOs, many of whom are teachers and Anganwadi workers.
It said 23% of BLOs surveyed received no training, while 38% of those who received training were trained for less than a day. More than 80% reportedly said they could not cope with the workload.
The report also referred to the deaths of five BLOs, which it attributes to work pressure and mental distress. The circumstances and causes of those deaths would require independent verification.
Notices and Form 6
The report stated that 43 lakh voters received notices — 23 lakh over alleged non-mapping with the 2002 electoral roll and another 20 lakh under the “Logical Discrepancy” category.
It also records 7,70,988 Form 6 applications submitted by September 24, covering both restoration requests and new voters. The committee said the figures warrant closer examination as the revision process progresses.
The report has called for an independent assessment to establish the extent of any wrongful exclusion from the electoral rolls.
Speaking at the release of the report, actor and social activist Prakash Raj demanded that the SIR of electoral rolls in Karnataka be completely scrapped. He asserted that the issue extends beyond elections or political victory, alleging that an attempt was being made to “divide the country into two”.
A delegation of the Anti-SIR Coalition, led by the actor, met Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar at his residence on Wednesday and handed over the SIR Scrutiny Report to him.

briefs.headline: SIR: Filled Form-7 targeting Muslim voters surface in Belagavi; BLOs allege they were pressured to sign
briefs.deck: BLOs allege they were pressured to sign, and say that two men, claiming to be from the Belagavi City Corporation, brought a bulk of Form-7 applications seeking deletion of only Muslim names.
briefs.bodyText:
“For at least the last 15 years, I have been the Booth Level Agent (BLA) here at polling station 196 in Belagavi North Assembly constituency. But last week, when I saw at least 380 Form-7 applications at the school, I was shocked to find my name and my brother’s, along with those of our relatives and neighbours, sought to be deleted,” said Meersab Sanadi, BLA at Veerabhadra Urdu Model School in Belagavi’s 7th Cross, where he is also the chairman.
The incident, in which “already printed” bulk Form-7 applications seeking deletion of Muslim names were received by Booth Level Officers (BLOs), was reported at at least six polling stations in Belagavi North Assembly constituency — four in Veerabhadra Nagar (polling parts 194, 195, 196 and 199) and two at the Government Kannada Higher Primary School in Shettigali (polling parts 209 and 210).
BLOs at these stations told The Hindu that two men, claiming to be from the Belagavi City Corporation, brought a bulk of Form-7 applications seeking deletion of only Muslim names. The voters’ names and other details were pre-filled, while the objectors’ names were either handwritten or left blank.
The men allegedly repeatedly told the BLOs that the applications had to be signed and returned urgently. The BLOs, however, refused, saying they knew the electors whose names appeared on the forms as that they had been living in the area for years. When the BLOs continued to refuse, the men allegedly called someone over the phone who posed as Electoral Registration Officer (ERO) Udayakumar Basavantappa Talawar and instructed them to sign the applications.
At the same time, Mr. Sanadi returned from lunch and questioned the two men after finding his name. “When the BLOs questioned the men, they were told that such forms had been sent to BLOs across polling stations and had to be signed urgently. The men then again called someone on the phone who posed as ERO and instructed the BLOs to sign the forms,” he maintained.
ERO Mr. Talawar confirmed to The Hindu that someone had falsely used his name and that he had not issued any such instructions.
Under pressure, some BLOs said they signed the forms, while others said they tried to contact their supervisors and the Assistant Electoral Registration Officer (AEROs), but could not reach them.
As the situation unfolded, the BLA said he and other local residents at the polling station contacted Belagavi North MLA Asif Sait, who was attending the Assembly session and could not be reached. They then contacted his son and Congress worker Amaan Sait.
Speaking to The Hindu, Mr. Amaan Sait said the men initially claimed to be from the corporation when he questioned them. When pressed further, they said they were from Dr. Ravi Patil Hospital, he said.
Mr. Sait said that when some of the objectors whose details were on the forms were contacted, they confirmed that the names and phone numbers were theirs, but said they had not filled out the applications against anyone. “The forms could be recovered at one polling station as it was immediately brought to the notice, but that couldn’t be done at other polling stations,” he said.
For instance, several forms were filed in Shashikant Jadhav’s name, but when contacted, he said the EPIC details and number on the forms were his, but he had not filled out any of the forms.
Deletion requests even after deadline
The trend of seeking deletions of Muslim voters’ names, meanwhile, continued in Bhalki even after the claims and objections period ended on September 23, with people who had filed Form-7 applications in bulk before the deadline continuing to file applications. The statutory Form-10 report shows 1,131 applications were received between September 24 and 29, of which 1,123 were bulk filings.
Applications filed after the claims and objections period will be taken up only after the final electoral rolls are published on October 27.
Chief Electoral Officer (CEO) V. Anbu Kumar was not available for comment.

stories.headline: Oil prices stay flat as markets weigh US-Iran talks and Middle East supply
stories.deck: Despite slight changes in oil prices today, Brent and WTI Crude both experienced gains in their last trading sessions. Investors remain alert to the evolving US-Iran negotiations, as their outcomes are likely to sway market dynamics. Furthermore, Saudi Arabia has restarted oil tanker loading activities via its East-West Pipeline. Recent statistics presented a mixed bag regarding US crude…
stories.bodyText:
Oil prices showed little movement in early trading on Thursday after both major benchmarks gained about $1 a barrel in the previous session. The oil market remained calm as investors weighed developments in US-Iran peace talks and the recovery in Middle East crude exports.
Around 7 am IST, WTI Crude was trading at $90.16 a barrel, down 26 cents, or 0.29%, while Brent Crude stood at $97.93 a barrel, lower by 10 cents, or 0.10%.
The largely flat session came after a strong September for oil prices. Brent has gained around 14% this month, marking its biggest monthly rise since July. WTI, meanwhile, has advanced about 5% over the month.
Markets are also assessing the outlook for crude supplies from the Middle East as they track the latest developments around US-Iran peace talks. The movement in prices remained limited in early Thursday trading despite the gains recorded by both benchmarks in the previous session.
The direction of WTI could depend on developments around the US-Iran negotiations. A new catalyst, such as progress in peace negotiations, will be needed for WTI to break below the immediate support level of $88 a barrel, he added.
Qatar on Tuesday said that it hoped shuttle diplomacy between Tehran and Washington could result in a breakthrough. 
The comments came as uncertainty continued around the possibility of a deal between the two countries.
US President Donald Trump, meanwhile, denied reports from Axios and CNN that cited US officials as saying he was prepared to offer Iran sanctions relief and release frozen Iranian funds in exchange for "concrete" steps from Tehran on its nuclear programme.
The oil market is also tracking the pace at which supplies from the region are returning. Saudi Arabia resumed oil tanker loadings from Yanbu on Tuesday after restarting its East-West Pipeline.
Gulf exports have also recovered, according to Goldman Sachs. The bank estimated that Gulf oil exports, including "dark exports" involving ships operating with their location transponders turned off, had reached 23.3 million barrels per day over the last week. That is in line with the 2025 average, while exports doubled in September, Goldman Sachs said in a note on Tuesday.
Production policy is another factor in focus ahead of the OPEC+ meeting on Sunday. Two people with knowledge of the matter told Reuters that OPEC+ oil-producing countries are likely to leave their November oil production targets unchanged.
US inventory data offered a mixed picture for the market. Crude stocks increased by 922,000 barrels to 427.3 million barrels in the week ended September 25, the Energy Information Administration said. At the same time, fuel inventories fell sharply, with the decline coming amid strong seasonal and global demand.

stories.headline: Google restricts access to new AI model over safety concerns
stories.deck: Google said Argon is designed to refuse requests that could help carry out cyberattacks or develop chemical, biological or nuclear weapons
stories.bodyText:
Google on Wednesday (September 30, 2026) said it would withhold its most powerful artificial intelligence model from the public for now, releasing Gemini 4 Argon only to a vetted group of cybersecurity experts to avoid misuse by hackers.
"Safely releasing frontier capabilities at this level requires a phased approach," wrote Koray Kavukcuoglu, Google's chief AI architect, in a blog post announcing the model.
Google said it is voluntarily giving the U.S. government early access to the model and will gather feedback from testers before making it widely available.
The cautious rollout mirrors the approach of rival Anthropic, which has kept its most advanced model, Claude Mythos Preview, restricted to a small number of trusted organizations.
Washington briefly forced Anthropic to suspend access to its publicly released Claude Mythos and Claude Fable models in June, and has since set up a voluntary process for vetting the most powerful AI models before release.
The announcement came a day after President Donald Trump hosted top tech executives, including Google chief Sundar Pichai and Anthropic's Dario Amodei, at the White House, where they signed a voluntary accord pledging to police the risks of their own AI systems.
Cybersecurity experts fear the state-of-the-art technology could be used to hack banks, hospitals and government systems.
Google said Argon excels at complex tasks in software engineering, legal and financial work and cyber defense, with a leading ability to find and fix critical software flaws.
Early testers used Argon to uncover a flaw in software used by hospitals around the world that exposed sensitive personal information — something other advanced models had missed, Google said.
Google said Argon is designed to refuse requests that could help carry out cyberattacks or develop chemical, biological or nuclear weapons.
Anthropic and ChatGPT-maker OpenAI have built similar safeguards into their most advanced models.
Google said it is monitoring the model's reasoning to stop it from straying beyond what users intended, a risk researchers call misalignment.
The issue has taken on new urgency since OpenAI disclosed in July that two of its models, including one not yet released, broke out of a sealed test environment during a cybersecurity evaluation and hacked into the servers of AI company Hugging Face.

stories.headline: Trump, AI majors pledge AI safety; experts flag lack of enforcement
stories.deck: Accord calls for internal controls, independent audits and board oversight, but experts flag weak enforcement, lack of common safety standards and concerns over auditor independence
stories.bodyText:
U.S. President Donald Trump and the heads of six major technology companies have signed a voluntary accord committing frontier AI developers to a four-layer system of safety controls, including internal monitoring, independent external evaluations and board-level oversight.
Also read | AI doomsday debate: What are AI researchers and critics afraid of?
The “White House Accord on Super Intelligence: Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities” was signed by Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, xAI CEO Elon Musk and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.
The accord says companies training and deploying frontier models should put in place internal controls to monitor their models’ capabilities and alignment, including risks involving cybersecurity, biosecurity and chemical threats. The controls should also ensure that AI models do not hack or access technical systems in unintended ways.
Under the second layer, companies are expected to have an internal team responsible for ensuring that controls, monitoring and detection systems work as intended and that identified problems are addressed.
The third layer calls for an independent external auditor or evaluator to assess whether these controls are working as intended. The fourth requires an independent board committee to oversee the teams responsible for controls and audits and ensure that identified problems are addressed.
The participating companies will also meet regularly to establish safety standards and best practices. The accord says that, over time, these measures could be codified into laws or regulations.
The voluntary nature of the commitment, however, has raised questions about how effective the framework can be when safety requirements come into conflict with commercial considerations.
‘Positive step, but consequences are missing’
Gaurav Vasu, founder of Unearthinsight, described the accord as a positive step because it brings together internal checks, external audits and board oversight.
But its effectiveness would depend on whether companies actually act on safety findings, particularly when fixing a problem could delay a product launch or affect revenue.
“The document does not set deadlines or specify consequences for failing to follow through,” Mr. Vasu said.
He said the success of the accord should ultimately be judged by whether companies “fix serious problems before release and delay launches when necessary.”
Mr. Vasu also raised questions about the independence and functioning of the external audits. These include who selects the auditor, what information the auditor can access, who sees the findings and what happens if a company does not act on them.
He also drew a distinction between checking whether a control works as intended and checking whether it provides enough protection. The accord, he said, does not establish a common minimum safety standard.
He called for common safety standards, deadlines for fixing serious findings, stronger auditor-independence requirements, reporting of serious incidents and legal powers to require corrective action or restrict unsafe releases.
‘Audits cannot replace continuous assurance’
Vaibhav Tare, Chief Information Security Officer at Fulcrum Digital, said board-level oversight was a necessary step, but AI governance could not remain limited to policy documents and periodic audits.
As AI systems become more autonomous, security controls should be built directly into their architecture, with clear ownership, least-privilege access, continuous monitoring and auditable decision trails.
Organisations need to know where AI is deployed, what systems it can access and what actions it is authorised to take.
“Independent audits should therefore complement continuous technical assurance rather than replace it,” Mr. Tare said.
‘A voluntary commitment can only go so far’
V Ramgopal Rao, Vice-Chancellor of BITS Pilani, called the accord a useful first step, particularly because AI development is moving faster than regulation.
He said the agreement could help establish common industry practices quickly. But its effectiveness would depend on audit transparency and what companies do when serious safety concerns are identified.
“A voluntary commitment without consequences for non compliance can only go so far,” Prof. Rao said.
He also pointed to an inherent conflict that companies competing to build and release increasingly powerful AI systems are simultaneously being asked to decide whether those systems are safe enough.
Independent audits could help, but he said there needed to be clarity over who selects auditors, what standards they use, how much access they receive and whether findings are made public.
“If every company defines safety differently, an audit can easily become a procedural exercise rather than a meaningful test of risk,” he said.
Prof. Rao said some of these voluntary commitments would eventually need statutory backing, including clearly defined safety standards, independent audits and mandatory reporting of serious incidents. Regulators should also have the technical expertise to assess AI systems themselves.
‘Companies cannot each define their own safety’
Karthik Vaidhyanathan, Assistant Professor at IIIT Hyderabad and a researcher at the intersection of AI and software engineering, described the accord as a step forward but said it was not sufficient by itself.
He compared AI safety with aviation, where companies do not certify their own aircraft. Independent certification authorities, auditors and standards bodies are involved.
Allowing every AI company to interpret broad safety requirements in its own way, he said, could undermine the purpose of the framework.
“We need certification authorities, which are standardised at a much larger scale,” Prof. Vaidhyanathan said.
He called for broader international standards, with different safety thresholds for safety-critical applications, healthcare and less consequential uses.
He also said AI safety should not be assessed only at the model level. The systems in which models operate need their own safeguards. An AI model might recommend an action, but the surrounding system should determine whether that action can actually be executed.
“AI safety is also an engineering problem,” he said, arguing for multiple layers of safeguards across models and systems.
He favoured international safety protocols involving multiple countries and organisations rather than a single global AI safety regulator, warning against excessive centralisation and gatekeeping.
‘A voluntary accord remains an illusory promise’
Anandaday Misshra, Founder and Managing Partner of AMLEGALS, said the four-tier structure was conceptually sound but questioned whether a voluntary commitment could provide meaningful accountability.
“A voluntary accord remains an illusory promise,” Mr. Misshra said.
His principal concern was a structural conflict of interest that the company sets the benchmark, retains the auditor and holds the audit report.
“If a structural conflict of interest arises within this architecture, the external auditor will merely verify if controls function as intended,” he said.
Mr. Misshra also pointed to the 2023 White House AI commitments, which he said suffered from loose drafting and uneven adherence. In a competitive market, he argued, commitments without penalties could come under pressure.
He called for a statutory regulator with powers to inspect and penalise, objective public standards, auditors insulated from client fees and mandatory public disclosure. He also said the eventual effectiveness of the framework would be influenced by the continuing competition between US and Chinese AI companies in frontier models.
For India, Mr. Vasu said, the accord does not create new legal obligations for Indian companies. It could result in additional testing and compliance work for Indian IT services companies, but it is too early to regard it as a major revenue opportunity because the accord primarily concerns companies developing and deploying frontier AI models.

briefs.headline: Senior citizen wrongly paid tax on Rs 25.42 lakh bond interest; ITAT orders Rs 9.91 lakh refund
briefs.deck: Each year, the senior citizen reported the interest earned from his investments in tax-free bonds under the ‘exempt income’ category in his income tax return (ITR). But made a mistake in one year. The man realised the error only after the deadline for filing a revised ITR had passed. He therefore approached the jurisdictional assessing officer (JAO) and filed a rectification application.
briefs.bodyText:
What if you end up paying taxes on a tax-free income? Will you be refunded? In one such case a senior citizen man erroneously ended up paying tax on his interest earnings. A senior citizen living in Gurugram invested Rs 3 crore in two government tax-free bonds in 2013.
Here’s what the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT) Delhi ruled.
What the case is about
Each year, the senior citizen reported the interest earned from his investments in tax-free bonds under the ‘exempt income’ category in his income tax return (ITR). However, while filing his return for AY 2022-23, he mistakenly treated Rs 25.42 lakh in interest from the bonds as taxable income from other sources.
This included Rs 16.96 lakh that he earned from IFCL bonds and he got Rs 8.46 lakh from REC bonds. As a result, he ended up paying Rs 9.91 lakh in income tax. He was, however, not required to pay this amount since the investments by their definition were tax-free.
However, the man realised the error only after the deadline for filing a revised ITR had passed. He therefore approached the jurisdictional assessing officer (JAO) and filed a rectification application under Section 154 on January 19, 2024.
But, the JAO rejected this request from the senior citizen. The JAO took the view that a claim for such a deduction could not be considered by the JAO except through a revised ITR. 
The officer relied on the Supreme Court's decision in Goetze (India) Ltd. v. CIT.
The Commissioner of Appeals (CIT A) upheld this decision.
The senior citizen then challenged the matter before the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT) Delhi.
Why did the senior citizen win the case?
The ITAT Delhi observed that the rectification requested by the senior citizen was aimed at correcting an error apparent from the existing record and did not amount to making a new claim.
The tribunal held that the ruling in Goetze (India) Ltd., which the AO had relied on while turning down Bakaya’s rectification application, did not apply to the present case.
The ITAT referred to the coordinate Bench’s decision in the case of Kapil Dev Nikhanj, where it was held that the Goetze India decision referred to (supra) only limits the assessing authority from entertaining a fresh claim when it was not made in a valid return. It does not curtail the powers available to appellate authorities, as was clearly stated in the final paragraph of that judgment.
Following the earlier ITAT decision, the Delhi tribunal therefore ruled in the man’s favour. It directed the AO to treat the Rs 25.42 lakh interest earned by the senior citizen from the IIFCL and REC tax-free bonds as exempt income under Section 10(15)(iv)(h).
The ITAT further held that once the interest from these bonds was accepted as tax-exempt, the assessing officer was required to issue a refund of the resulting excess tax of Rs 9.91 lakh to the man, together with interest as admissible under the law.
As a result, Bakaya succeeded in the case and will receive a tax refund of Rs 9.91 lakh.
Chartered Accountant Ashish Niraj, Partner, A S N & Company, told ET that Section 10(15)(iv)(h) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, provides a complete exemption from income tax on any interest income that is earned from tax-free bonds and debentures issued by specified public sector companies. These include NHAI, REC, IIFCL and IRFC, among others.
So simply put, the interest income from such bonds is fully exempt from tax in the hands of the taxpayer, without any limit. Despite this, the senior citizen inadvertently treated the exempt interest as taxable income in his ITR and ended up paying an additional Rs 9.91 lakh in tax.
Niraj said that in this case, the assessing officer himself acknowledged the error in an order dated April 7, 2025, stating that the income from the bonds "was erroneously added as taxable income while filing the income tax return."
The ITAT Delhi also took note of the AO's report and the fact that interest from IIFCL and REC tax-free bonds is exempt under Section 10(15)(iv)(h) of the Income-tax Act. The tribunal therefore held that the amount could not be taxed, in view of Article 265 of the Constitution of India.
Niraj said a simple clerical mistake should not result in a tax liability when the underlying income is itself exempt from tax. The ITAT allowed the man’s appeal and directed that the excess tax be refunded.

briefs.headline: PNGRB bats for level playing field across EV, CNG and LNG vehicles
briefs.deck: The senior official at PNGRB mentioned the level-playing field could be instituted either through required and suitable taxation, subsidies or infrastructure, among other things.
briefs.bodyText:
A level-playing field across vehicle types — from electric vehicles (EVs) to compressed natural gas (CNG) and liquefied natural gas (LNG) — is essential to ensure consumer economics work for each segment, said Anjani Kumar Tiwari, Member, Petroleum and Natural Gas Regulatory Board (PNGRB).
Speaking to The Hindu on the sidelines of the launch of The Energy and Resources Institute’s (TERI) comparative assessment of vehicular fuels, Mr. Tiwari said consumer economics must remain central while framing policies for all fuels.
“Economic consideration is important for consumers. At the same time, it is important to have a level-playing field for all vehicle technologies,” he said.
According to him, such parity could be achieved through a mix of appropriate taxation, subsidies, infrastructure support and policy interventions. Without a balanced framework, he said, consumers would find it difficult to compare the true economics of different vehicle options.
The TERI-PNGRB report aims to address these gaps by identifying areas where infrastructure creation, incentives and tax structures need alignment across fuel categories.
“Where infrastructure is required to be created, where incentives are to be accorded or tax rates must be made similar across the board. These are some of the things that would help carve a level-playing field and is what the report seeks to put forth,” he said, adding that leaving any segment unattended would make the overall paradigm “unbalanced”.
On recent CNG price increases, he attributed the pressure to higher input costs following the renewed conflict in West Asia. India’s immediate priority, he said, was ensuring fuel availability.
“Once that [disruptions because of the West Asia crisis] stabilises, prices will eventually come down and ultimately passed on to consumers,” he added.
Mr. Tiwari also highlighted the role of compressed biogas (CBG) in reducing India’s dependence on imported gas. Under the government’s target of setting up 5,000 CBG plants by 2030, the sector could contribute significantly to domestic gas availability.
“If these 5,000 plants operate at 50% capacity, around 30-40 million metric standard cubic metres per day (MMSCMD) of gas could be produced, depending on the [feedstock] yield,” he said.

briefs.headline: IRDAI’s proposed distribution norms ruffle feathers of LIC agents, broker body
briefs.deck: Cost efficiency should not be pursued in a manner that reduces the number of active agents or makes the profession economically unsustainable.
briefs.bodyText:
Voicing concerns over the impact of the reforms IRDAI is proposing to norms governing distribution, commissions and expenses, bodies representing insurance brokers and Life Insurance Corporation of India (LIC) agents have urged the insurance regulator to consider the likely repercussions on the jobs and livelihoods.
Cost efficiency should not be pursued in a manner that reduces the number of active agents or makes the profession economically unsustainable. The primary objective of distribution reform should ultimately be to increase insurance coverage and improve policyholder outcomes, said the Life Insurance Agents’ Federation of India (LIAFI) in its responses to IRDAI.
Any substantial reduction in the earnings potential of agents could discourage new entrants and adversely affect the existing agency force, Secretary General B. Markandeyulu said.
The federation highlighted the role of LIC agents in strengthening the insurance movement in India and said the agency channel remains crucial for expanding insurance access. LIAFI represents several lakh agents of the state-owned insurer.
Favour strict action against frauds
While supporting strict action against deliberate fraud, unethical practices and genuine cases of mis-selling, LIAFI said “regulatory measures should differentiate between intentional misconduct and genuine errors or situations beyond an agent’s control.”
The federation said commissions are the primary source of livelihood for individual agents and should be viewed as fair compensation for professional services rendered, rather than merely as a cost to be reduced. It added that, with employment generation being a national priority, the regulatory framework should ensure that insurance agency remains an economically viable profession.
Demand grandfathering provisions
Any change in commission structures must be based on a comprehensive assessment of the actual services, responsibilities and cost involved. “We request that appropriate grandfathering and transition provisions be incorporated, particularly in relation to existing business and continuing servicing responsibilities,” Mr. Markandeyulu said.
Expressing concerns over the consultation paper ‘Recalibrating economics of insurance distribution’ that IRDAI has opened for public comments, the Insurance Brokers Association of India (IBAI) said it supports the regulator’s stated objectives of policyholder protection, transparency, curbing mis-selling and wider insurance coverage. But the more than thirty separate commission caps by product and channel, together with a one-third cut in insurers’ overall expense limit will harm the very policyholders it seeks to protect.
Reduce reach to small towns
“Insurance is a people business. The [consultation] paper will reduce the people who reach customers in small towns and the people who service them inside insurers, and it contains no mechanism to ensure that the savings reach policyholders as lower premiums,” the IBAI said, attributing it to an unnamed spokesperson.
In a release, IBAI, which represents 798 licensed insurance brokers, said it will file its detailed response by October 25 and urge IRDAI to retain the 2023 expense-of-management framework, confine caps to coerced-choice sales, require premium refunds to customers where such segments run low claims ratios and publish an impact assessment before drafting regulations.
