briefs.headline: Cabinet approves ₹1.86 lakh crore Green Energy Corridor to evacuate 135GW renewable energy
briefs.deck: Green Energy Corridor initiative will strengthen India’s Intra-State Transmission System to enable evacuation of up to 135 gigawatt (GW) of renewable energy across States/Union Territories
briefs.bodyText:
The Union Cabinet on Wednesday (September 30, 2026) announced the third phase of the Green Energy Corridor (GEC) that seeks to integrate up to 135 gigawatts of renewable energy into grids across States and Union Territories by fiscal year 2032-33.
The scheme would further strive to address curtailment, that is a situation when grid operators limit the power output from renewable sources to maintain grid stability.
The Hindu had reported August 10 that the government was in the final planning stages of instituting the third phase of the GEC. It had learnt that it was awaiting Union Cabinet’s nod for approval.
Project outlay
The third phase of the scheme accounts for a total project outlay of more than ₹1.86 lakh crore.
This comprises of ₹1.36 lakh crore for developing intra-state transmission systems (InSTS) in the third phase.
As a first, the latest phase of GEC also provisions a ₹50,000 crore-dedicated component for deploying 50 GWh of battery energy storage system (BESS).
It carries central financial assistance (CFA) of ₹54,082 crore for offsetting intra-state transmission charges and keep the power costs down.
Among other things, the CFA institutes ₹45,005 crore towards offsetting costs relating to intra-State transmission system and ₹6,000 crore for battery storage.
All greenfield projects under the InSTS component would adhere to a tariff-based competitive bidding (TBCB) mode while brownfield projects entailing upgradation and network strengthening would be executed adhering to cost-plus-basis (CPB) model.
Committee formed to expedite pending projects
In a press handout, the Ministry informed that a dedicated joint coordination mechanism would be instituted at the Cabinet Secretary level for monitoring project progress on a half-yearly basis.
Speaking to the press, Santosh Sarangi, Secretary at the Union Ministry for New and Renewable Energy (MNRE) informed that pending projects under the second phase of the GEC would fall into the Committee’s purview.
Mr. Sarangi also stated that only one project is pending completion under the first phase which is expected to conclude end of fiscal year 2027.
The second phase is expected to complete end of FY2028, he added.
More States coming in
The previous phases of the GEC enrolled more than 10 States including Andhra Pradesh, Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and Tamil Nadu with Kerala and Uttar Pradesh enrolled in the second phase.
Mr. Sarangi further informed that applications of two more States, that is, Mizoram and Bihar are being evaluated by the Central Electricity Authority (CEA).

briefs.headline: Centre’s fiscal deficit at end-August hits 41.9% of 2026-27 target on higher subsidy spends
briefs.deck: Total expenditure stood at 38.9% of the budget estimates as of August 2026, as compared to 37.1% in the same period of 2025-26
briefs.bodyText:
An increase in subsidy spending, particularly on fertilisers, has led to the Centre’s fiscal deficit reaching 41.9% of its budgeted target for 2026-27 as of August 2026, compared to 38.1% at this point last year.
Data released by the Controller General of Accounts on Wednesday shows that the Centre’s total revenue stood at ₹13.7 lakh crore in the April to August 2026 period of this financial year, while its total expenditure stood at ₹20.8 lakh crore during the same period.
Total receipts were largely in line with the trend of last year, making up 37.5% of the budget estimates for the year as of August 2026 as compared to 36.7% in the same period of last year.
Total expenditure, however, stood at 38.9% of the budget estimates as of August 2026, as compared to 37.1% in the same period of 2025-26. Within this, revenue expenditure stood at 38% of the full year’s target compared to 36.7% at this point last year.
“This is up mainly due to higher allocations for fertilisers, petroleum, and food distribution, which is the subsidy component,” Madan Sabnavis, chief economist at the Bank of Baroda said. “In the case of fertilisers, it was 60% of the total budget relative to 50% last year.”
However, capital expenditure also grew faster this year than last year. As of August 2026, total capital expenditure stood at 41.7% of the budgeted target of ₹12.2 lakh crore for the year. It had been 38.5% at this point last year.
“Given that the economy is expected to grow by a little over 7% in real terms and above 11% in nominal terms, the fiscal deficit ratio should largely be contained in the region of 4.5-4.6% this year assuming some slippage in non-tax revenue due to the OMCs not generating profit,” Mr. Sabnavis said.

stories.headline: Harita Bhadra eyes 22.45s and World Championships after two Asian Games medals
stories.deck: Harita Bhadra arrived at the Asian Games chasing a podium finish and left Nagoya with two bronze medals, in the women’s 200m and mixed 4x100m relay. Her first senior international competition has also sharpened the next target: a 22.45-second run, the qualifying mark for the 2027 World Championships. Bhadra reflects on the races, the mental lessons from Nagoya, her relay experience and why she…
stories.bodyText:
Before the Asian Games, Harita Bhadra had a fairly modest definition of success. A personal best, she had said, would make her happy. A podium finish was what she wanted to chase.
She will now leave Aichi-Nagoya with two bronze medals - one from the women’s 200m and another from the mixed 4x100m relay, where she ran the anchor leg as India set a national record of 41.06 seconds.
“I’m very happy because I got like two medals at the end of the day. Getting on the podium is like one of the best feelings, especially when you’re representing India, and you’re getting a medal for your country. So that was a very surreal experience for me,” Bhadra told Timesofindia.com from Japan.
“And I didn’t get a personal best, but considering the weather conditions and everything, I feel like I gave my best. So that’s okay,” she added.
It was also Bhadra’s first senior international competition representing India. She had not been through a junior international programme in Indian colours before arriving in Japan, so much of what she encountered in Aichi-Nagoya was new - the scale of the stadium, the pressure of the races and the closeness of the competition - but she found out quickly that training cannot reproduce all of that.
“I’ve definitely learned a lot from this competition and definitely even discovered a lot about myself actually,” she said. 
“Such scenarios [can be experienced] only in competition, and the level of the pressure and the level of execution will only increase as you go higher and higher.”
“But I discovered how strong I can be mentally. If I tell my mind to do something, it can do it.”
Before the race, Bhadra knew she belonged
Watching Bhadra through the Games, there was a noticeable contrast. Before the races, she was quiet and composed, but her expressions would change once she crossed the line. The happiness was immediate.
“On the start line, my only mindset is that I belong over here,” she replied when asked what he goes through between those two moments.
“I don’t have to be scared of any of my competitors because, even I’m on the same start line. I just try to trust my body, and I’m not thinking about anything because I’m just staying in the moment, and I’m just trusting my body that all the work I have done is like my body is ready to execute it.”
That composure, however, did not mean the nerves had disappeared before her 200m final. Rather, Bhadra says she was nervous. The Reliance Foundation-backed athlete had already given herself a good platform in the heats, finishing second with 23.31s, behind Singapore’s Shanti Pereira.
“Everybody on the start line is nervous, but you just accept it. You’re nervous, but that doesn’t mean you’re not confident at the same time. It’s just a mix of both things: you can be nervous but also be equally confident at the same time.”
The 200m bronze came down to 0.01 seconds
The finish, though, was nerve-racking - to say the least. Pereira won in 22.78s, with China’s Chen Yujie taking silver in 22.93s. Bhadra crossed in 23.20s, but Japan’s Abigeirufuka Ido was only 0.01 seconds behind in 23.21s. That meant the bronze was decided by the narrowest of margins, with the photo finish separating Bhadra from the Japanese sprinter.
For a few seconds after the finish, Bhadra was unsure where she had finished. She had expected the results to appear on the screen opposite the finish line. After the race, she went across to teammate Unnati Aiyappa and sat with her. Unnati eventually pointed towards another screen. “She was like, ‘You have come third’, and that’s when I realised that I have come third.”
The medal was secure, but the race itself still had things Bhadra wanted to improve. “You will never be satisfied with a race. There is always something you will feel that, okay, this could have been done better. This part could have been executed better,” she said.
For the 23-year-old, more international exposure should help with that. The stage was completely new, and she felt there were sections of the race she could have handled better.
“I know I had more left in me, but I trust the process, and I trusted that whenever I know I can, I will execute that race that I have in my mind.”
One part of the race, though, had given her evidence that the work was moving in the right direction. The last 30 metres, something which had worked on, with her coach Rohit Mane at Reliance Foundation.
“Yes, definitely, because I think I won the race because of the last 30 metres. So that improvement was clearly there.”
Bhadra’s coach Mane was not in Japan for the Games, but they stayed in touch through video calls and regular calls, while the relay group had the support of Reliance Foundation’s Martin Owens and James Hillier, along with the AFI coaches, around them in Japan.
The coaches, she said, kept reminding the four runners that the work had already been done and that they had to trust the runner alongside them. “They kept us motivated to like trust each other. And that's how we also trusted our partners more.”
The relay brought a different kind of pressure
By the time Bhadra returned to the track for the mixed 4x100m relay, she had already raced twice. The stadium was no longer unfamiliar.
“I was definitely more confident because I had, like, two races' experience,” she said. “I knew now how it’s going to feel like, on the start, and I knew how I will feel stepping into the stadium and everything, how the call room is.”
“I was more calm and settled because I was familiar with the environment, basically. So going into the relay, I felt more collected than I was in 200.”
The quartet of Gurindervir Singh, Sneha Shanuvali, Animesh Kujjur and Bhadra had been working on the event well before arriving in Nagoya. The Asian Games camp in Bhubaneswar in August, followed by an acclimatisation camp in Tsukuba.
They trained the relay twice a week during the camp. As the Games approached, that came down to once a week because all four athletes also had individual events to prepare for.
Bhadra ran the anchor leg in both the semifinal and final, producing strong finishes on each occasion. In the semifinal, she had to recover after a difficult baton exchange on the bend, but still produced the run that carried India into the final. In the medal race, her late surge again proved crucial as India secured bronze. The decision to use Bhadra as the anchor, she says, was made by the coaching staff and AFI team.
“They decided to give me the anchor leg. So I was like, okay, I will do the anchor leg. That’s it.”
The semifinal did test that decision almost immediately. Kujur fell during the baton exchange before Bhadra took the baton and glanced back for a fleeting second, but with the baton in hand, she focused on the job at hand.
“My only thing was I have got the baton. So he [Kujur] has done his job of giving me the baton. So my job is to make the team qualify. As soon as I finished, I was just looking out, like just trying to understand what actually happened. I was trying to see if Animesh is okay or what actually happened.”
Studies can wait. The next number is 22.45
There was another decision from earlier in the year that Bhadra had wanted to test properly: putting her studies on hold and giving sprinting her full attention.
She had not made the decision because she could not handle both. She wanted to find out what would happen if she did not have to divide her time.
“I just wanted to give myself the chance to explore how it would be like. I only have to just focus on track and I don’t have to juggle two things at once,” she said.
Track, she said, requires time and dedication. “I am very happy with the decision. It was a good decision. I’m happy I gave myself the opportunity to explore how it would be.”
Her family being in Japan made the week different too. She had wanted them to see her compete at a major event, and they were there for it.
“I actually loved it that my family was there because I was just so excited that they are going to see me run at such a big event, like one of the biggest events of my athletics career so far,” she said.
“I was very happy they could be there with me because it just made everything like 100 times more special.”
Having ticked one of the big markers for this year, Bhadra is eyeing higher goals now, and her next target is already clear.
“I am chasing to qualify for the World Championships in 2027.”
The World Championships and eventually the Olympics, which had seemed further away before Aichi-Nagoya, now feel a little closer too. “Yes, definitely. It’s a step closer to, like, step higher, step closer. The qualifying mark is 22.45s for 200 metres.”
She believes it is achievable. Bhadra’s personal best in 200m currently stands at 23.14s, which she clocked in June this year.
“It is doable. But yeah, it is closer but still a lot of work to do there,” said Bhadra, pausing briefly before answering.
The area she wants to work on most is not the one a stopwatch will immediately show. It is the mental side. “On the starting line, before even starting the race, if you are mentally not strong, you have lost the race. Everybody is so close, like I said, 0.01 seconds. Like, it’s like nothing.”
Her answer is to stay calm enough to keep competing when the race is still there to be won. “You have to have that mental thing of not giving up, of believing that, ‘No, I can still win.’”
She still wants to take it one day at a time
For Bhadra, being mentally calm and connected to the race is now part of the work alongside the physical preparation. She is not planning to choose between the 100m and 200m just yet.
The two events, she says, complement each other. Training for the 100m helps the 200m, and vice versa. She will take an off-season before her coach puts together the next plan.
As for a favourite?
“I have my days of choosing 100 and some days of choosing 200. I can’t choose for sure.”
The medals have not changed the way she wants to approach the next season either. Before the Games, Bhadra had spoken about taking things one day at a time. She still uses the same approach now, even with the attention that will come after two Asian Games medals.
“I really don’t think about expectations. Over there, I’m just running for myself. I’m not running for anybody else. The only thing is, yes, every day has to be an improvement, even if it is little. But my only goal is to take it one day at a time and to improve from the previous day,” she said.
For now, there is no elaborate celebration planned. Her family is staying in Japan for a few more days to explore the country. Once she returns, Bhadra wants to meet her coach and ‘show off’ the two medals. Then there will be family and friends at home.
And then there is Dagina.
The handmade jewellery brand Bhadra started in October 2025 will turn one next month. She designs and makes the pieces herself and, because it remains a hobby, handles the work on her own. The Asian Games build-up and the last two months in camp meant she had not been able to spend much time on it.
She had started Dagina as a way of taking her mind away from athletics. Now Japan has given her an idea for what comes next.
“Now, once I’m back, I’m going to start again, maybe do a collection inspired by Japan or something like that.”

stories.headline: Asian Games 2026: Andhra athletes win three golds, a bronze
stories.deck: Jyothi Surekha and Ganesh Mani Ratnam clinch gold in compound archery; woman cricketer Sree Charani brings gold; Satwiksairaj and Srikanth are in men’s badminton squad that wins bronze
stories.bodyText:
Athletes from Andhra Pradesh have bagged three gold medals and a bronze at the Asian Games in Japan so far, with archery, cricket and badminton all contributing to the tally.
Nine athletes from the State are competing, according to Ramana, Section Officer (Associations), Sports Authority of Andhra Pradesh. They are badminton players P.V. Sindhu, Satwiksairaj Rankireddy, Kidambi Srikanth and Kavipriya Selvam; cricketer Sree Charani; archers Dhiraj Bommadevara, Thirumuru Ganesh Mani Ratnam and Jyothi Surekha Vennam; and hurdler Jyothi Yarraji.
On Wednesday, (September 30, 2026) Jyothi Surekha and Ganesh clinched gold as India swept all three compound archery team titles at Okazaki City. Jyothi Surekha, with Chikitha Taniparthi and Prithika Pradeep, beat China 238-234, equalling the world record. Ganesh, from Naidupeta in Tirupati district, joined Kushal Dalal and Sahil Jadhav to edge China 238-237 after overcoming South Korea in the semi-final.
President Droupadi Murmu told the women’s team that their “precision, composure and teamwork have made the nation proud”. Of the men’s win, she said, “Completing a clean sweep of Gold across all three Compound Team events, Indian archery has achieved a remarkable feat.”
Prime Minister Narendra Modi said the women’s win “is even more special because their performance also equalled the World Record”. Union Sports Minister Mansukh Mandaviya called the men’s gold “a proud moment for Indian archery and for the entire nation”.
Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu said Ganesh’s “path from Naidupeta to international glory stands as a testament to what focus and hard work can accomplish”. Deputy Chief Minister K. Pawan Kalyan said the women’s team had “brought the Tricolour to the highest podium”. IT Minister Nara Lokesh called Ganesh’s journey “a matter of immense pride for our State”.
The men’s badminton team won bronze. Every member of the squad, including Satwiksairaj and Srikanth, receives a medal, Mr. Ramana said. India lost 3-1 to China in the semi-final at Ichinomiya.
For Jyothi Surekha, Wednesday’s gold is her sixth medal across four consecutive Asian Games: four gold, one silver and one bronze. “Her experience is a major advantage,” said her father, Surendra Kumar, speaking from Vijayawada.
Sport runs in the family, he said. She began swimming as a child and, at five, swam across the Krishna, a feat recorded in the Limca Book of Records. She took up archery at 12. “Because we have seen her go through that experience from childhood, her achievements do not seem entirely unexpected to us,” Mr. Surendra Kumar said.
The Volga Archery Academy in Vijayawada, run by Cherukuri Satyanarayana, has produced several of the State’s leading archers. Mr. Satyanarayana, Vice-President of the Archery Association of India and chairman of the A.P. Archery Association, attributed the archers’ success to discipline, concentration and timing.
Among its trainees is Dhiraj, who set an Asian Games record of 698 in the recurve ranking round and has reached the individual quarter-finals and the team semi-final.

stories.headline: Asian Games 2026: Pakistan edge India to take 2-0 lead in volleyball quarterfinal
stories.bodyText:
India's Mansi advanced to the women's 62kg quarterfinals with a convincing 6-1 win over Kazakhstan's Irina Kuznetsova.
Mansi opened her account with a point awarded for an illegal grip before adding two more points early in the second round to move 3-0 ahead.
The Indian held on to complete a 6-1 victory and book her place in the quarterfinals, where she will face South Korea's Subeen Jo.
Pakistan defeated India 3-0 in the men's volleyball quarterfinal to end India's campaign at the Asian Games.
Pakistan took the opening set 25-19 before edging a closely fought second set 25-23. They then closed out the contest with an 18-25? Wait, Pakistan wins 25-18, to complete a straight-set victory.
India's wait for a first Asian Games medal in men's volleyball since 1986 continues after the quarterfinal defeat.
Chan Sin Yuk edged Anahat Singh in a thrilling five-game battle as Hong Kong moved 1-0 ahead of India in the women's squash team semifinal.
Anahat raced into a 2-0 lead after winning the opening two games 11-9 and 11-8, but Chan fought back to take the third 11-6. The Hong Kong player then saved Anahat's chances in a dramatic fourth game, winning 13-11 to force a decider.
Chan eventually prevailed 12-10 in the fifth game to complete a 3-2 victory (11-9, 11-8, 6-11, 11-13, 10-12).
It was a tough defeat for Anahat, who had led by two games and had four match balls but could not close out the contest.
India's Aman Sehrawat pulled off a remarkable comeback to beat Mongolia's Borgil Tuvshinbaatar 8-6 in the men's Greco-Roman 77kg round of 16 and advance to the quarterfinals.
Aman took the first point but Borgil responded to lead 2-1 at the end of the opening round. The Mongolian then extended his advantage to 6-1 with a four-point move after securing a strong grip.
With a minute remaining, Aman had cut the deficit to 4-6 before producing a stunning burst of scoring moves to turn the bout on its head and move 8-6 ahead.
He held on in the closing moments to seal a memorable comeback victory. Aman will face Qatar's Shahin Badaghimofrad in the quarterfinals.
Anahat Singh made a strong start against Sin Yuk Chan, edging the opening game 11-9 after the two stayed close at 8-7. The Indian was vocal in celebration after taking the lead.
The second game was just as tight, with the scores level at 8-8 before Anahat produced three straight points to win 11-8 and move 2-0 ahead.
Chan fought back in the third as Anahat briefly lost her rhythm. The Hong Kong player opened up an 8-4 lead and went on to take the game 11-6.
Anahat regained control in the fourth, racing to a 6-3 advantage and earning three match points. But Chan fought back brilliantly to level at 10-10, before another match point slipped away.
India's Aman has begun his round-of-16 bout against Mongolia's Borgil Tuvshinbaatar, taking the opening point to move 1-0 ahead.
Borgil responded quickly to turn the score around, ending the first round with a 2-1 lead. The Mongolian then produced a big scoring move, securing a strong grip on Aman to collect four points and stretch his advantage to 6-1.
India's Rupa Bayor has been eliminated from the women's individual poomsae event after finishing fifth in her semifinal.
Bayor scored 7.6100 in the second semifinal, which featured eight competitors. Only the top four advanced to the gold medal round, leaving the Indian just outside the qualifying positions and ending her campaign.
India finally ended Pakistan's five-point streak but remained a point behind at 20-21. Joel Benjamin then produced a superb spike to bring India within one at 21-22.
Pakistan earned two set points at 24-22 after a Musawer spike, but Ashwal Rai kept India's hopes alive with a strong finish from the net to make it 23-24.
However, India could not stop Usman's decisive spike, with Pakistan taking the second set 25-23 and moving 2-0 ahead in the quarterfinal.
India have hit back strongly in the second set after a successful review helped them level the score at 13-13. Ashwal Rai then produced some inspirational play as Jerome Vinith's side surged three points clear at 16-13.
Pakistan responded with two quick timeouts and soon erased the deficit, drawing level at 16-16. India called a timeout of their own and immediately found another run, scoring three straight points to move 19-16 ahead.
But the momentum swung again as Pakistan rattled off five consecutive points to take a 21-19 lead. The second set is now finely poised, with India needing to find another response to stay in the contest.
Already assured of a medal, India's women's squash team will look to go a step further this time and book a place in the final, improving on its performance at the Hangzhou 2022 Asian Games.
Anahat Singh is the first Indian in action, taking on Sin Yuk Chan in the opening singles.
India have made another strong start in the second set, edging ahead 6-5 with an ace from Joel Benjamin.
Pakistan's blocking has continued to pose a major challenge for India, who may need to vary their attacking approach and add more unpredictability to their spikes.
The second set remains finely balanced, with the teams level at 13-13.
Pakistan continued to pile pressure on India in the opening set, extending their advantage despite India's attempts to fight back.
Chirag produced a clever moment of deception, shaping up for a powerful spike before opting for a slower shot that caught the Pakistan defence off guard. But India could not turn such moments into a sustained comeback.
Pakistan led 20-14 and moved further ahead after India's timeout, making it 22-15. They eventually closed out the first set 25-19 to take the early advantage in the quarterfinal.
It has been a closely fought opening set between India and Pakistan, with the two sides locked at 9-9 after an even start.
Pakistan have now created the first significant gap of the quarterfinal, pulling six points clear at 20-14. India face a crucial stretch as they look to stay alive in the opening set.
India have made a quick recovery after Pakistan started the men's volleyball quarterfinal strongly. Pakistan moved 4-2 ahead early on, with their blocking at the net proving effective.
India responded with three straight points to turn the game around. Captain C. Jerome Vinith produced an ace during the run as India moved 5-4 ahead in the opening set.
India's Anish Bhanwala is back in action in the men's 25m pistol rapid qualification, with Stage 2 now underway. The Indian shooter will be aiming to finish among the finalists after putting himself in contention in the opening stage.
Bhanwala scored 290 points in Stage 1 on Wednesday, a tally that left him fifth in the standings. He is the only Indian in the field and will now look to build on that performance in Stage 2 and secure his place in the final.
India's Chikitha Taniparthi suffered a heartbreaking quarterfinal exit after Nurisa Dian Ashrifah of Indonesia edged her 144-143 in a tense women's individual contest.
Chikitha had taken the lead going into the final set, but a costly 8 on her opening arrow allowed Nurisa to regain the advantage. The Indonesian followed it with a perfect 10, while Chikitha could manage only a 9.
The Indian finished the final end with 27 points, and although she hit a 10 with her last arrow, it was not enough to overturn the deficit. Nurisa's 9 secured a one-point victory and ended Chikitha's run.
The defeat also brings India's campaign in the women's individual section to an end. India had entered the event as the defending champions.

India’s campaign at the 20th Asian Games, Aichi-Nagoya 2026, continues on Thursday, with athletes competing across several sports.
India will compete in shooting, boxing, Table Tennis, archery, squash, and many other events. There will also be medal opportunities for the Indian contingent.

briefs.headline: Sanju Samson says constant meetings and activities keeping India ‘switched on’
briefs.deck: India's rain-truncated match against Japan in Sano went down to the wire after the contest was curtailed due to a wet outfield.
briefs.bodyText:
Incessant rains have deprived India of crucial training and competition time in Japan, but constant meetings and team activities have helped the players remain "switched on", said opener Sanju Samson here on Wednesday (September 30, 2026).
India have been in Japan for the past 10 days but have only played a five-overs-a-side game against Japan on September 22. The three-time T20 World Cup winners have their first proper training session scheduled later on Wednesday.
Earlier, India's opening match in the Asia Games — a quarterfinal against Afghanistan — was abandoned after no play was possible due to rain. India will take on Sri Lanka in the semifinal here on Thursday.
"We have had some good time [off the field]. We have been doing some team activities. We were trying to do some practice (but the weather did not allow). But we were training and conditioning in the gym," Samson said when asked if the weather has disrupted the team's rhythm.
"We were spending time together. We were talking [about] cricket and combinations. We were having constant meetings to switch on the players when it is required.
"… these are the times where we need to be a bit more aware that we need to switch on and suddenly play a big semifinal. We all are aware of that. Luckily, we have got a good sunny day today to practice," said Samson on the eve of the semifinal against a second-string Sri Lanka.
Samson said the players are itching to take the field with the weather keeping them indoors mostly.
"Yes, yesterday we were having a chat in the gym. When the team is having a gym session, we are saying that 'yes, we need to get out and play some game of cricket'. So, we all are very much excited to come and play a proper game of cricket."
The outfield is expected to be soft and the pitch sluggish considering the wet weather.
Asked if it was safe to play in such conditions, Samson said: "Conditions are a bit different. We have never played a game here in Nagoya. Most of us are playing here for the first time, so there might be a lot of unknown factors. And it goes for the other team as well. So, both teams are coming here fresh.
"We don't know the conditions until we go out there and play a proper game of cricket. So, that is where the fun is. I think that is where any team can compete against any team."
India's rain-truncated match against Japan in Sano went down to the wire after the contest was curtailed due to a wet outfield.
India are playing a three-match ODI series against the West Indies simultaneously, besides a men's 'A' series against Australia at home.
Asked about the depth of Indian cricket and the ability to field multiple teams at the same time, Samson said, "It is a known fact nowadays how strong Indian cricket has grown from last so many years. So, I think there has been some constant effort. I think definitely IPL plays a huge role.
"But I feel our domestic cricket is also playing a huge role actually. We have been constantly making great efforts to go out and play all the domestic matches whenever we get a chance. And that is where we tend to develop a lot of talents also."

briefs.headline: Sunil wins second Asian Games medal with bronze; Nisha Dahiya knocked out
briefs.deck: Sunil had won a bronze in Hangzhou 2023 Games, ending a 13-year wait for India for medal in the Greco Roman style.
briefs.bodyText:
Sunil Kumar became the first Indian Greco Roman wrestler to win two Asian Games medal after clinching a bronze in the men's 87kg event but Nisha Dahiya endured a medal-less campaign on the opening day of the wrestling competition here Wednesday (September 30, 2026).
Sunil assured his podium place with a technical superiority win (9-0)over Philippines' Roberts Callum Johnston, who was no match to the strength and technical skill of the Indian.
Locking his rival's right arm, Sunil effected two take downs to quickly open up a 4-0 lead. A defensive Johnston was put on ground in 'Par Terre' position from where Sunil made more scoring moves to finish the bout in the first period itself.
Sunil had won a bronze in Hangzhou 2023 Games, ending a 13-year wait for India for medal in the Greco Roman style.
Before that Ravinder Singh and Sunil Kumar Rana had won bronze in 2010 Guangzhou Games.
The 27-year-old Haryana wrestler was left to fight for a bronze medal after losing his semifinal by technical superiority to Japan's Taizo Yoshida.
This was after he began with a confident technical superiority win over Tajikistan's Muhammad Sultonzoda.
Against Sultonzoda, the Indian finished the job in a jiffy after his rival was put on a 'par terre' position for being defensive. Sunil made full use of the advantageous ground position to employ consecutive gut wrench moves.
In the last-four bout, Yoshida led 6-0 after the first period and added five more points to move to the gold medal match, not giving a single scoring opportunity to Sunil.
"I am happy but not satisfied because I already have a bronze medal at Asian Games. I made a mistake against the Japanese and paid the price. I used strength more than technique " Sunil told PTI.
"Coach Hargobind had studied my opponents well and we followed a strategy. Credit to him. I will now try to qualify for the Los Angeles Olympics through the Asian Qualifier," he added.
Hargobind Singh praised Sunil for executing the 'two-on-one' grip well.
"He used to bring this 'two-on-one' grip into the bouts but struggled to convert that into scores. Here he did well to score points, so well done. He tried to use it against the Japanese also and even had a grip on his waist but left his arm a bit loose to let him effect a shoulder throw," he told PTI.
"He lost points on counter. We will work on these mistakes. We have a very good chance in 97kg tomorrow. We are expecting Nitesh to win a medal. He has a good path to final," the coach added.
Aman (77kg), Sumit (60kg) and Nitesh (97kg) will be in action in Greco Roman while Mansi Ahlawat will be on mat in women's 62kg on Thursday.
Nisha Dahiya knocked out
However, disappointment was in store for Nisha Dahiya, who blew away lead in her both women's 68kg bouts to make an early exit.
In her opening bout, Nisha lost to North Korea's Pak in the 1/8 round and later the repechage round to bow out.
Nisha had moved ahead 2-0 but Pak executed a four-pointer to end the first period with a 4-2 lead.

briefs.headline: Squash at Asian Games: Indian men and women assured of medal
briefs.deck: The Indian men, top seed and defending champions, collected a 2-0 win over Kuwait in the quarterfinals.
briefs.bodyText:
Indian men's and women's teams eased into the semifinals of the Asian Games with convincing wins over Kuwait and Singapore respectively, assuring themselves of a medal here on Wednesday (September 30, 2026).
The Indian men, top seed and defending champions, collected a 2-0 win over Kuwait in the quarterfinals.
Among the two singles, Veer Chotrani had to dig deep against Bader Almogghrebi before prevailing 12-10, 8-11, 11-0, 11-5 in a 34-minute contest.
Abhay Singh, India's highest ranked player and silver medallist in the singles competition, sealed the tie 11-3, 11-4, 11-8 win over Ammar Altamimi.
After the match, Chotrani said he did not play up to his potential against Kuwait.
“I didn’t have the best day, I didn’t play my best squash at all. Tomorrow is a new day, and I will hopefully be better tomorrow (for the semifinal)," he said.
"“Of course, Abhay was really strong (today). Tomorrow we have to play as a team, support each other. It’s not going to be easy. Most likely we will draw to play Malaysia, so it’s going to be tough in all three matches. We will just give it our best.”
In the women's singles, the Anahat Singh-led team tamed Singapore 2-0 in its quarterfinal.
Starting the proceedings, Tanvi Khanna produced a gritty show, eking out a 11-6 4-11 15-13 11-1 win over Au Yeong Wai Iynn in a thrilling 32-minute opening singles match.
In the second singles, 18-year-old Anahat, who bagged a silver in the individual event, then thrashed Au Yeong Wai Yhann 11-7 11-3 11-4 in just 22 minutes to complete the victory.
Veteran Joshna Chinappa, who also won a bronze in the mixed doubles event, didn't need to take the court.
The women's team will face Hong Kong in the semifinals scheduled for Thursday while the men will meet Malaysia.
India had blanked Iran 3-0 in its last group-stage match on Tuesday after defeating both China and Japan in their first two matches of Pool C.

briefs.headline: Ronaldo leaves Portugal camp, promises truth 'in due time', wishes team-mates luck
briefs.deck: Cristiano Ronaldo has left Portugal’s camp ahead of Thursday’s Nations League clash with Denmark following a dispute over his role under new head coach Jorge Jesus. Ronaldo confirmed his departure after Jesus said he would not start the match. The 41-year-old has not announced his international retirement, but said he would reveal the reasons for his decision “in due time.”
briefs.bodyText:
Cristiano Ronaldo has abruptly left Portugal’s national team camp one day before the UEFA Nations League meeting with Denmark, after a turbulent few days involving his role under new head coach Jorge Jesus. The 41-year-old confirmed his departure in a statement on Wednesday, saying he would reveal the reasons “in due time” while wishing Portugal and his team-mates good luck. Whether the decision marks a farewell to international football remains to be seen.
Ronaldo confirms he has left Portugal camp
Ronaldo confirmed his departure from the Portugal camp on Wednesday, September 30, in a statement posted on his official social media accounts. The announcement came as Jesus held a press conference ahead of Portugal’s match against Denmark in Copenhagen. The Portugal captain said his decision followed the coach’s comments and a conversation with Proença, who had changed his schedule to travel to Copenhagen as tensions over Ronaldo’s role in the team grew.
“After the National Team coach's press conference, and following a conversation with the President of the Portuguese Football Federation, I have decided to leave the National Team training camp,” Ronaldo wrote.
He then indicated that he would explain what had happened at a later stage.
“In due time, I will tell all Portuguese people the truth about the reasons that led to my departure from the national team, to which I have always dedicated myself.”
Ronaldo finished by wishing Portugal and his team-mates well.
“Now is the time to wish good luck to Portugal and to all my team-mates, without exception.”
The Portuguese Football Federation confirmed that Ronaldo had left the camp, while saying the remaining squad would continue preparing for the Denmark match and the subsequent Nations League fixture against Norway.
Ronaldo was seen leaving Parken Stadium in a Portuguese Football Federation vehicle as his team-mates arrived for training, according to Portuguese newspaper A Bola. His private jet was also reported to have been preparing to take him away from Denmark. Reuters later reported that the aircraft had left Madrid for Copenhagen and was scheduled to return to the Spanish capital.
Ronaldo remians Portugal's most-capped player and leading scorer, with 234 appearances and 146 goals for his country.
Jorge Jesus had told Ronaldo he would not start against Denmark
The dispute developed after Ronaldo was left on the bench for Portugal's 2–1 Nations League victory over Norway.
Jesus selected João Félix and Gonçalo Ramos in attack, with Ramos scoring Portugal's winning goal after Erling Haaland had equalised. Ronaldo warmed up during the second half but was not introduced.
Jesus had previously said he wanted to manage Ronaldo's workload after the forward played almost 70 minutes against Wales in Portugal's opening Nations League match.
Ronaldo then went directly to the dressing room after the Norway victory rather than joining his teammates in celebrating with the travelling supporters.
The situation continued into Portugal's preparations for Denmark.
Portugal's head coach Jorge Jesus speaks during a news conference in Copenhagen, Denmark, Wednesday, Sept. 30, 2026, ahead of their Nations League soccer match against Denmark. (Liselotte Sabroe/Ritzau Scanpix via AP)
Jesus said on Wednesday that Ronaldo would train with the team, while also confirming that he would not start against Denmark.
“Yesterday, he did not refuse to train,” Jesus said.
“Francisco Conceicao did not train because he was injured, and Joao Felix because we tried to ease his fatigue, while Cristiano did work in the gym. Today he will train. It is the fourth day, so he will train.”
Jesus then explained the decision he had made over Ronaldo's role.
“I can promise what I want. I am the coach. I told the player that he would not start the match, and that he would be on the substitutes' bench.”
“If I need him for 30 minutes then he will play, and if I do not need him then he will not play.”
Jesus also made clear that nobody would influence his selection.
“No player will change my mind, neither him nor anyone else in football, not even any president, that will never happen.”
Ronaldo left the camp after the press conference.
Pedro Proença travelled to address the situation
The Portuguese Football Federation president changed his schedule and travelled to Copenhagen as the situation around Ronaldo and Jesus escalated.
Proença held talks with the parties involved on Wednesday morning after the disagreement that followed Ronaldo's omission against Norway.
Jesus had maintained that there was no major problem between himself and Ronaldo and said his conversations with the captain had been normal.
Ronaldo, however, had missed three consecutive training sessions according to 
A Bola
, despite Jesus saying shortly before his departure that he expected the forward to train.
Portugal's Cristiano Ronaldo arrives for training in Copenhagen, Denmark, Wednesday, Sept. 30, 2026, ahead of their Nations League soccer match against Denmark. (Liselotte Sabroe/Ritzau Scanpix via AP)
The Portuguese newspaper reported that Ronaldo left the Parken Stadium in a Portuguese Football Federation vehicle as his teammates arrived for training.
His departure came only minutes after Jesus' press conference.
Earlier reports had said Ronaldo was unhappy with the decision to leave him out against Norway and with the uncertainty surrounding his starting place against Denmark.
Ronaldo's retirement remains unconfirmed
Portugal now face Denmark on Thursday without Ronaldo in the squad, with the team leading Nations League Group A4 after two victories.
Portugal have six points, three clear of both Denmark and Norway.
Ronaldo's departure does not amount to an official retirement announcement. He has not said that he is ending his international career, while the Portuguese Football Federation has not announced his retirement.
His final words before leaving camp, however, have prompted immediate questions because he said he would reveal the reasons for his decision later and then wished Portugal and all his teammates good luck.
Ronaldo has spent more than two decades representing Portugal, becoming the country's record appearance holder and scorer while winning the 2016 European Championship and the 2019 Nations League. Whether Wednesday's decision represents another dispute that can eventually be resolved or the beginning of the end of his international career remains unanswered.
For now, Ronaldo has said only that he will tell the Portuguese people the truth “in due time”.

briefs.headline: Too shy for stardom, too good to ignore: Meet Chikitha Taniparthi, Indian archery’s latest golden girl
briefs.deck: Every archer knows the wait between release and arrival, that held breath when nothing can be changed and everything is decided. For Chikitha Taniparthi, that wait lasted years. It began in a backyard, ran through lockdowns and a snapped bowstring, and ended in Japan with a double gold.
briefs.bodyText:
By now, the two gold medals she has snapped up at the 2026 Asian Games have catapulted the extremely shy compound archer Chikitha Taniparthi into the national headlines. The 221-year-old – who comes from a modest farming family in Peddapalli, Telangana – is a stranger to stardom and the sprinkling of opulence that sporting achievements usually carry along in India.
There are no fancy routines or competition-day playlists yet. She doesn’t even carry a pair of earphones. All she has is a burning hunger to become India’s most decorated archer ever. And she’s off to quite a start.
For all the reticence, Chikitha – a huge Mahesh Babu fan – finds inspiration in films that are of a more audacious ilk.
“There was a movie Ram Charan did last year called Game Changer. After watching that – and it usually happens when I watch certain films – I thought, what should I do or learn from this? I myself should change the game where I am,” Chikitha told The Hindu a few weeks before setting out to Japan for the Asiad.
“Now, everyone says, whatever rank Chikitha is in, she will somehow change the game and come up. Similarly, I watched a film called Biker, where the message blared, ‘No fear.’ It all registers somewhere.”
Of betrayal and faith
That itch to push beyond the ordinary is a Taniparthi family trait. Her father, Srinivas Rao – a huge sports enthusiast – combed newspapers for summer camps his own childhood never offered.
“Naanna (father) didn’t have any such facilities when he was growing up, so he was keen to ensure that I had access to all that, within our means.”
In school, Chikitha tried her hand at a multitude of options including volleyball, badminton, basketball and kho kho. But Srinivas wanted his child to pursue an individual discipline. Towards that end, she earned a black belt in karate. But archery was destined to be the one to stick with.
“Team sports are riddled with politics. Since archery is an individual game, whatever we do is directly visible and we do what we do for ourselves.”
The year was 2018. Chikitha’s uncle, on her father’s request, had got her a recurve bow from Decathlon with which she trained behind her house, shooting at haystacks. Eventually, she and a few of her classmates went to the Police Training Center to try and find a coach to teach them. There, someone asked her to switch to a compound bow and took money from Srinivas for the same, only to disappear without a trace.
ALSO READ | At peace with pressure: Understanding Jyothi Surekha
Disappointed but not disillusioned, the father and daughter persisted with the sport. Chikitha moved away from recurve and towards compound.
“Recurve bow needs a lot of practice and power. You need to train every single day. If you return after resting for a few days, you’ll see so many changes and will have to rework it all. With compound, I could train for two hours each in the morning and evening. It needed the archer to set themselves mentally and keep getting better.”
The next pursuit became trying to purchase a compound bow, but the COVID-19 pandemic arrived soon after.
“Our classes all went online, so I could train every day. At that point I didn’t know what a national medal was, but I wanted to win one.”
“During Covid, my father had set up a target and a 50m path so I could shoot. He would go to the field every morning. My brother and I would go running every morning along the edges of our field. That is when I became really fit. In fact, my father also joined us and improved,” Chikitha recalled. “Eventually I left for Sonipat, and my father settled back into the duties of the house. The family’s fitness streak sort of snapped there.”
Srinivas pushed beyond his means to support his daughter’s dream. He even sold the family’s paddy harvester. Meanwhile, YouTube videos formed the bedrock of Chikitha’s technical base, and one of the archers she grew to idolise – Abhishek Verma – would become her mentor.
Eventually, the District Collector’s office sanctioned funds for a compound bow. As she looked for a coach and a good training centre, Chikitha chanced upon the contact details of My Choice Archery Store, an equipment outlet run by Abhishek and his wife Sonali in New Delhi.
Guiding light
“I got her number from the shop they run and I knew she was Abhishek anna’s wife. He and his coach (Lokesh Chand Pal) agreed to take me in for training at the Yamuna Sports Complex for five days.”
This was in August 2021. As the world found a way to open up again, so did Chikitha’s prospects as an archer. Her uncle chipped in with funds for the trip to the capital.
There, Abhishek told Srinivas to leave Chikitha’s well-being to him.
The first goal was a sub-junior medal.
“I didn’t know much about archery, but I used to watch Abhishek anna’s videos and check with my father if I was getting things right. Anna then told me that my strength was good, but he changed my anchor technique. In the mornings, he used to let me shoot 50-100 arrows. In the evenings, there would be no shooting. We just trained holding the bow and arrow in place. This was to develop patience. I learnt all my basics there at the Yamuna Sports Complex.”
Chikitha entered the senior nationals in preparation for the sub-junior event and got a very low score there. Her mentor had notes, and the pair eventually struck off the first box in what would become a long checklist of turfs to conquer.
She then participated in selection trials to make it to the Sports Authority of India’s National Centre of Excellence in Sonipat. There, coach Vivek Kumar took her under his wing. “After my father, he is the only person I open up to after tournaments and cry with,” Chikitha said.
“In 2021, I was in Hyderabad for the National Ranking Archery Tournament. Abhishek told me that there was a talented girl I should meet. Her father brought her to the hotel we were staying in. This girl was so small and frail. I asked her if she wanted to go to Sonipat. She nodded in agreement, but there were tears too,” Vivek told The Hindu.
Nonetheless, he persisted. “If a player like Abhishek recommends someone, you cannot ignore that. He told us she would become a good archer like Jyothi Surekha.”
Abhishek, it turned out, was right. The parallels between Chikitha and Jyothi are endless. Both are introverts by nature, content to shuttle between the training field and the gym. Both follow instructions to the letter, even when that means shooting 300-odd arrows, and both are always early, rain or shine.
ALSO READ | Indian archers hit the bullseye with three gold medals at 2026 Asian Games
Vivek remembers Chikitha clinging to her father until the moment they parted. Slowly, Sonipat won her over. By night, she had found the courage to make a request: biryani. The coaches understood how hard it is for someone from South India to move to a diet where rotis reign, and they indulged her.
Any doubts about her potential evaporated at the trials ahead of the 2022 Asian Games. She missed qualification but finished a commendable seventh, enough to convince her coaches that she could be shaped into an athlete who would make India proud on the global stage.
Chikitha’s reasons for liking archery are threefold. “First, because, as my dad wanted, it’s an individual sport. Second, archery is a sport where I can concentrate and focus with no distractions. Third, Anna told me, ‘You are a champion, and you will continue to be.’”
Others’ faith in her sowed the seeds of Chikitha’s ambitions; formal training is teaching her to nurture them herself. That process has not been without its hiccups. In 2024, Chikitha struggled to place among the top 16 and lost motivation mid-season.
“That period was a struggle and I couldn’t accept it. Before the national games, I wanted to get selected, but I was nowhere near the top. I was working with high poundage, and I said if I hit any more (shooting arrows), I might get injured. I didn’t feel like shooting. It took me some time to recover from that. I went to Tirupati, tonsured my head, prayed very hard,” she recalled.
“I have to get Abhishek anna the Asian Games plushie. I want to be able to buy another harvester for my father. The World Championships are next year. World Cups are there and then the Olympics are there in 2028. Anna told me to approach everything step by step and not put everything on my mind and take stress. Anna and Jyothi akka are consistent faces in the Indian team. I want to be able to do that too.”Chikitha Taniparthi
Through every hardship, Chikitha never once thought of abandoning archery. When her first substantial prize money arrived, after the 2023 National Games in Goa, she spent it on arrows, stockpiled for practice. A fresh set every few months is her idea of a treat.
“It is not about the money; it does not matter as long as the results come my way.”
It’s taken a village to get Chikitha out of Peddapalli and onto the world stage. Even efforts to watch her favourite Mahesh Babu on OTT is a family activity. OTPs for streaming apps will come from siblings nearly 1500km away. When she comes home for a few days every now and then, there is no TV for the family to unwind with together. She returns to a big family welcome, the open paddy fields and a progressively controlled anxiety of missing training.
Ask Chikitha what she is proud of and, along with the golds, she may mention the gift of deep sleep. Thunder can rattle every window, but she will slumber on.
“I don’t get sleep only when thoughts come to me, which happens when everything is silent.”
Then she went to Japan and became the lightning. Whether or not she slept through the aftermath, India did not. Two golds flashed across the sky, and a sport that thought it knew its stars blinked in the glare.

briefs.headline: For TN vice-captain Andre, pressure is a privilege
briefs.bodyText:
For C. Andre Siddarth, pressure is a privilege. The soon-approaching task of serving as R. Sai Kishore’s deputy in the Tamil Nadu Ranji Trophy team is not bogging the 20-year-old down.
The leadership role which has been bestowed upon him is, in fact, driving the young gun to unlock new features in his game. “Becoming the vice-captain for a State like Tamil Nadu at 20 is a privilege and honour. The pressure that comes with it is a blessing,” said Andre, who will also lead TN U-23 in a clash against Rest of India U-23 starting here on Thursday.
“I just want to elevate myself. It (the experience) will be a great learning for me,” added the right-handed run accumulator while also expressing admiration for Tamil Nadu teammate B. Indrajith and former Australia skipper Steve Smith.
Now that Andre is set to shoulder additional responsibility, he is likely to deal with even more peaks and valleys. “Ups and downs are part and parcel of the sport, so being level-headed is important. I am not worried about the result: I am only worried about my improvement.”
He is relishing working under new head coach V. Yo Mahesh, someone who has given wings to TN youngsters’ dreams.
“Yo Mahesh is pushing us out of our comfort zone. He is being hard: he wants us to do the right things, which I feel is much needed going into a new season. Ninety per cent of the practice sessions feel like a match... they are so intense”.

briefs.headline: Gill on the double as India hunts down 406 in style
briefs.deck: In reply to West Indies’ highest-ever ODI score of 405/7, India rode on Gill’s 233 not out off 133 balls (26 fours, 8 sixes) and Rohit’s 35th century (101 off 75 balls; 10 fours, 6 sixes) to a famous win, with the openers putting on 255 runs for the first wicket.
briefs.bodyText:
Through the global financial crisis, Arab Spring, the discovery of the Higgs boson, humanity’s first image of a black hole, a pandemic that brought the world to a halt, and the rise of generative AI, the world has not seen a successful ODI chase in excess of 400.
The last such chase came in March 2006. On Wednesday (September 30, 2026), Shubman Gill’s forensic artistry (223 n.o., 133b, 26x4, 8x6) and Rohit Sharma’s slouching grandeur (101, 75b, 10x4, 6x6) came to the fore as India finally joined that rare club. Chasing down 406 with eight wickets to spare, India took an unassailable 2-0 lead in the three-match series against West Indies at the Barsapara Cricket Stadium.
There is something faintly García Marquez-like about Gill’s current form. The extraordinary keeps occurring with such regularity that everyone has stopped treating it as extraordinary. A hundred from him now feels like rain in Macondo: remarkable in isolation, almost routine in accumulation. This time, he doubled down on it - in double-quick time.
Gill’s batting was silk and shrapnel. His wrists were particularly persuasive, shuffling deep into the leg side before cutting through backward point, or flicking over midwicket with the ease of a samurai wielding a light sword. He used his feet repeatedly, dancing down to Roston Chase and Keemo Paul and launching sixes over square leg and cow corner. There was precision, too: a late slice between deep point and deep third, a pristine punch past cover, a full-faced drive that left mid-on stranded. Even the short ball was not safe - a 141.3-kph delivery from Alzarri Joseph disappeared into the stands off Gill’s signature short-arm jab. He reached his hundred off 62 balls, his 11th in ODIs, before going on to raise the fastest ODI double hundred, off 117 balls.
Together, Gill and Rohit added 255 runs, the second-highest opening partnership in ODIs for India.
Rohit once said that when he is batting well, he gets into good positions. Watch him on a good day and you see it. A slight adjustment of the feet, a quiet transfer of weight, a subtle alignment of shoulders and eyes. No reaching. No lunging. No rescue missions. Just a man arriving exactly where he needs to be, exactly when he needs to be there. The shot feels inevitable because the position was perfect.
Earlier, John Campbell wasn’t to be trifled with. After all, when a man treats a missed hundred as unfinished business, he is best given a wide berth. If his 60-ball 62 in the first ODI was useful, his 68-ball 101 (9x4, 5x6) here was punitive. Campbell, skipper Shai Hope (104, 94b, 8x4, 3x6), and Amir Jangoo (114, 77b, 13x4, 3x6) formed the Caribbean century cartel as West Indies posted 405 for seven.

briefs.headline: Gill's 223, Rohit's 101 power India to record 406-run chase against West Indies
briefs.deck: India became only the second team to chase a target of 400 or more in men's ODIs, after South Africa chased 438 against Australia in Johannesburg in 2006. India finished on 406 for two in 43.3 overs after West Indies had posted their highest ODI total of 405 for seven.
briefs.bodyText:
Shubman Gill's unbeaten 223 off 133 balls, the fastest double century in ODI history, and 
Rohit Sharma
's 101 helped India chase down 406 against West Indies in the second ODI in Guwahati on Wednesday. India completed their highest successful chase in the format with 39 balls to spare, winning by eight wickets and taking an unassailable 2-0 lead in the three-match series.
India became only the second team to chase a target of 400 or more in men's ODIs, after South Africa chased 438 against Australia in Johannesburg in 2006. India finished on 406 for two in 43.3 overs after West Indies had posted their highest ODI total of 405 for seven.
Gill remained unbeaten on 223 off 133 balls, hitting 26 fours and eight sixes, while Rohit scored 101 off 75 balls with 10 fours and six sixes. The opening pair added 255 runs for the first wicket, giving India a strong start to the chase.
Gill's innings was the highest individual score in an ODI chase and the highest by a captain in the format.
The 27-year-old had to deal with cramps and a painful neck during his innings, but continued to take the Windies attack apart. 
He now has 11 ODI hundreds in 69 matches.
Gill's innings came alongside Rohit, the only other batter to have scored multiple double-centuries in ODIs.
The conditions at Guwahati offered little help to the bowlers. However, batters still needed skill, discipline, intent, appetite and fitness to complete the chase. Gill's innings provided all of that as India completed the second successful 400-plus chase in ODI history in only 43.3 overs.
The conditions also put Kuldeep Yadav's figures of 2-65 from 10 overs into context. Kuldeep became the second-quickest Indian to reach 200 ODI wickets during the match. Part-time off-spinner Naman Dhir conceded only 38 runs in 6.1 overs before leaving the field after getting injured.
Earlier, centuries from John Campbell, Shai Hope and 
Amir Jangoo
 helped West Indies post their first 400-plus total in ODI cricket. Their 405 for seven surpassed their previous best of 389 against England in 2019.
Campbell set the tone after West Indies were sent into bat, reaching his century in 65 balls. He scored 101 off 68 balls, with nine fours and five sixes, as West Indies took advantage of India's inexperienced pace attack.
A self-confessed admirer of 
Chris Gayle
, Campbell channelled the inner Universe Boss perfectly, flaying the Indian attack with brute power and freedom in his 101 off 68 balls (9x4, 5x6).
Hope and Jangoo then kept the scoring rate around eight runs an over through the middle and late stages of the innings.
Hope played the role of both anchor and aggressor. He was dropped on 27 by Virat Kohli at short midwicket, with the ball bursting through his hands, and made the most of the reprieve.
The West Indies captain went on to score 104 off 94 balls, hitting eight fours and three sixes, as he kept the scoring rate high and prevented India from making a comeback.
Jangoo provided further support, combining controlled stroke-play with attacking shots. He reached his second ODI century in 69 balls and finished with 114 off 83 balls, including 13 fours and three sixes.
It was the first time West Indies had three centurions in the same ODI innings. However, they scored only 82 for five in the final 11 overs, a period that eventually proved significant as India completed the chase with relative ease.
